practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes counter-urbanisation?
A) People moving from rural areas to cities for work
B) People moving from cities to rural areas, often keeping city jobs
C) Cities expanding outwards into the countryside
D) Population growing inside city centres
practice_questions.marks: B) People moving from cities to rural areas, often keeping city jobs [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways UK rural and urban areas are linked.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Commuting — workers travel from villages and small towns to cities each day.
• Shopping — rural residents visit out-of-town centres or city high streets, while online deliveries reach remote villages.
• Services — rural patients travel to urban hospitals and universities for specialist provision.
• Resource flows — rural areas supply cities with water, food and energy.
[2 marks — 1 per link]

practice_questions.text: Explain how sphere of influence affects access to services in rural areas.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Specialist services such as A&E hospitals or universities have a high threshold population, so they cluster in cities like Manchester.
• Rural residents must travel further to reach them, sometimes over an hour by car.
• Lower-order services (corner shops, GPs) can survive in smaller settlements because their threshold is lower.
[3 marks. Mastering: clear cause-effect with named example. Secure: links threshold to access. Developing: identifies threshold only. Emerging: vague.]

practice_questions.text: Compare access to services in an accessible rural area and a remote rural area in the UK.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Accessible rural areas (e.g. villages around Bristol or Manchester) often have frequent buses, post offices and primary schools, whereas remote rural areas (e.g. Mid-Wales, upland Northumberland) have lost many of these services.
• Counter-urbanisation increases accessible rural populations and supports services, in contrast to remote rural depopulation that closes them.
• Both areas rely on the nearest city for hospitals, but accessible rural residents reach them in 20–30 minutes whereas remote ones may take over an hour.
• Online services partly close the gap for both, although broadband coverage is weaker in remote areas.
[4 marks — credit explicit comparison.]

practice_questions.text: Using a named example, explain how counter-urbanisation has changed a UK rural area.
practice_questions.marks:
Cotswold villages near the M5/M40 corridor are suitable. Students may include:
• Cheaper fuel and fast trains since the 1990s allowed professionals to live in villages such as Stow-on-the-Wold while commuting to Bristol, Birmingham or London.
• Working from home after 2020 accelerated migration into the area.
• House prices in Cotswold villages have risen well above the national average, pricing out many local young people.
• Demand for restaurants, shops and primary schools has grown in some villages, but in others second homes leave streets quiet during the week.
• Traffic, planning pressure and rural identity debates have all sharpened.

Mastering: developed explanation, named example, multiple linked impacts.
Secure: clear sequence with example.
Developing: change described but located detail thin.
Emerging: generic counter-urbanisation answer.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
‘Counter-urbanisation has done more good than harm to the UK countryside.’
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Counter-urbanisation has reversed depopulation in many villages, keeping schools, shops and pubs open.
• Newcomers often bring spending power that sustains rural businesses and tradespeople.
• Restoration of older property has preserved historic buildings.
• Working from home reduces long commutes and supports rural economies.

Arguments against:
• House prices in counter-urbanised areas have risen sharply, pricing out local young people.
• Some villages become commuter dormitories with empty streets midweek and limited community life.
• Increased traffic, road widening and second-home pressure can damage rural character.
• Remote rural areas not benefiting from counter-urbanisation continue to lose services and population.

Judgement: a strong response weighs the regeneration of accessible rural villages against the loss of affordability and community in some places, and the continuing decline of remote areas. Net good in some places, harm in others.

Mastering: sustained evaluation, named places, clear conclusion.
Secure: arguments on both sides with examples.
Developing: imbalanced or weak conclusion.
Emerging: list with no judgement.
[8 marks + 4 SPaG]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best defines life expectancy?
A) The total population of a country in a given year
B) The average number of years a newborn baby is expected to live
C) The number of births per 1,000 women each year
D) The percentage of girls enrolled in primary school
practice_questions.marks: B) The average number of years a newborn baby is expected to live [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe one indicator of gender equality.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: a clear indicator with brief development, e.g. the share of women in parliament shows whether women hold decision-making power; Rwanda has the highest share at over 60%. Secure: indicator named with limited development. Developing: vague reference to women's rights. Emerging: no specific indicator.

practice_questions.text: Explain why gender and health are useful measures of social development.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: clear chain — gender equality and health show whether national wealth is reaching ordinary lives; high GDP can hide poor health or unequal opportunities; rising life expectancy and girls’ school enrolment signal real improvements in everyday life. Secure: one mechanism with effect. Developing: states they are useful without explaining. Emerging: no link to social development.

practice_questions.text: Compare GDP and infant mortality rate as measures of development.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: explicit comparison using linking words on at least two points — both are widely used and easy to compare across countries, however GDP measures national wealth whereas infant mortality measures the chance of dying before age one; GDP can be high in unequal oil states whereas infant mortality reveals weak maternal care, sanitation and nutrition. Secure: one explicit comparison. Developing: lists features of each separately. Emerging: only one feature named.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a country can have a high GDP but low social development. Use a named example.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: developed account using a named country (e.g. Equatorial Guinea, Saudi Arabia, oil-rich Gulf states) showing that GDP is high because of oil or another resource, but wealth concentrates in an elite, women’s rights are limited, life expectancy may be low, and access to clean water and schooling is poor. Secure: named example with two indicators but limited locational detail. Developing: generic with one indicator. Emerging: vague reference without named place.

practice_questions.text:
“A single development measure can never tell the full story of how developed a country is.”
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument with named examples weighing the strengths of single measures (GDP per capita is comparable, easy to calculate, useful for policymakers) against weaknesses (hides inequality, ignores gender, ignores environment, e.g. Equatorial Guinea high GDP but low life expectancy) and the value of composite measures like HDI or a basket of indicators reaching a justified judgement (e.g. a single number is useful as a quick comparison but a basket gives the truer picture). Secure: balanced argument with one named example. Developing: one-sided or generic. Emerging: simple agreement or disagreement without evidence.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes GNI per capita?
A) Total goods and services produced inside a country
B) Total income earned by a country's residents (including from abroad), divided by population
C) Average life expectancy at birth
D) The percentage of adults who can read
practice_questions.marks: B) Total income earned by a country's residents (including from abroad), divided by population [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what the Human Development Index (HDI) measures.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for a developed description:
• A composite measure that combines GNI per capita, life expectancy and average years of schooling into a single score (1).
• Each country is given a value from 0 (lowest development) to 1 (highest), allowing fair comparison across regions (1).
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why GDP per capita can be a misleading measure of development.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks for a developed cause-effect chain:
• GDP per capita is an average that hides inequality — a small wealthy elite can pull the figure up while most people live in poverty (e.g. South Africa) (1).
• Much economic activity in lower-income countries happens in the informal sector and is not counted, so GDP underestimates real economic activity (1).
• It says nothing about life expectancy, education or quality of life — Cuba's GDP is low but life expectancy is around 79 years (1).
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Compare GNI per capita and HDI as measures of development.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Credit explicit comparison words:
• GNI per capita is a single economic figure measuring income, whereas HDI is a composite of income, education and health (1).
• GNI per capita is easier to calculate and update annually, in contrast HDI requires more data and lags behind (1).
• Both rank countries on a sliding scale, similarly placing them along a development continuum (1).
• HDI better reflects quality of life, whereas GNI better reflects raw economic power (1).
[4 marks — must include explicit comparison links]

practice_questions.text: Using a named example, explain how the development gap between two countries can be measured.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks for a developed answer with named countries and figures:
• Names two countries at different points on the continuum, e.g. UK and Bangladesh (1).
• Provides GDP per capita figures: UK around US$58,000, Bangladesh around US$2,600 in 2025 (1).
• Adds HDI scores: UK 0.94, Bangladesh 0.66 (1).
• Includes life expectancy: UK 81 years, Bangladesh 73 years (1).
• Identifies one further measure such as years of schooling or infant mortality (1).
• Concludes by recognising the gap is closing but remains substantial across multiple measures (1).
[6 marks — locational detail and named figures are essential]

practice_questions.text:
'A single economic figure such as GNI per capita is the best way to measure global development.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Use the StudyVault rubric.

Mastering: Sustained evaluation weighing GNI's strengths (clarity, comparability, World Bank classifications) against its weaknesses (inequality, informal economy, quality of life). Uses named country examples (Cuba, South Africa, China) with figures. Reaches a justified conclusion (e.g. GNI is necessary but not sufficient — must be paired with HDI or other measures).

Secure: Clear arguments for and against. Some named examples and figures. Conclusion partly asserted.

Developing: Some arguments on each side; examples generic ('a rich country', 'a poor country'). Limited weighing.

Emerging: Simple comments on GNI with no comparison and no examples.

In favour: GNI is updated annually, internationally consistent, easy to compare; underpins World Bank country categories; correlates strongly with most other indicators.
Against: hides inequality (South Africa); ignores informal sector (sub-Saharan Africa, ~85% informal); says nothing about life expectancy (Cuba); can mask environmental damage from rapid growth; should be paired with HDI to be useful.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes a honey pot site?
A) An area with no tourists at all
B) A small popular site that attracts large numbers of visitors
C) An entirely artificial landscape
D) A protected area where visitors are banned
practice_questions.marks: B) A small popular site that attracts large numbers of visitors [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two physical features that make UK upland landscapes distinctive.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Hard, ancient rocks such as granite or slate that resist erosion and form steep relief.
• Higher rainfall (often over 2,000 mm a year) producing thin, acidic soils and fast-flowing streams.
• Glacial features such as U-shaped valleys, corries or ribbon lakes.
• Steep slopes and high altitudes (over 200–900 m).
[2 marks — 1 mark per feature]

practice_questions.text: Explain how human activity has changed one UK landscape you have studied.
practice_questions.marks:
Lake District example. Students may include:
• Tourism has caused footpath erosion at sites such as Tarn Hows because thousands of walkers compress soil and kill vegetation.
• Second-home buying has pushed up house prices in villages such as Hawkshead, forcing young locals to move away.
• Farming has shaped the open fells through sheep grazing, which prevents trees regenerating.
[3 marks — 1 for a simple point, 2 for development, 3 for a developed point linked to a named place. Mark scheme: Mastering — sustained explanation with named detail. Secure — clear cause-effect with a place name. Developing — basic point with limited place reference. Emerging — generic point.]

practice_questions.text: Compare the physical characteristics of one upland and one lowland UK landscape.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Geology: the Lake District is built on hard volcanic rocks and slate, whereas the Norfolk Broads sit on soft chalk and clay.
• Relief: the Lake District is steep with peaks over 900 m, in contrast to the Broads which lie at or near sea level.
• Climate: rainfall in the Lake District exceeds 3,000 mm a year, whereas the Broads receive around 600 mm.
• Soils and farming: thin acidic soils in the uplands support sheep, whereas deep fertile soils in the Broads support cereals and reedbeds.
[4 marks — credit explicit comparison using words such as ‘whereas’, ‘in contrast’ or ‘similarly’. 1 mark per developed comparison.]

practice_questions.text: Using a named example, explain how visitor pressure can damage a UK landscape.
practice_questions.marks:
Tarn Hows in the Lake District is suitable. Students may include:
• Tarn Hows attracts over half a million visitors a year, well above its quiet carrying capacity.
• Heavy footfall compacts soil along paths, killing grass and mosses; rain then washes loose soil away creating wide muddy scars on the fellside.
• Cars overflow car parks and verges turn to mud, while litter blows into the tarn affecting wildlife.
• Honeypot pressure inflates house prices in nearby Hawkshead, pricing out local first-time buyers.
• Local shops shift towards tourist gifts and away from everyday goods, reducing services for residents.

Mastering: developed explanation with multiple linked impacts and accurate located detail.
Secure: clear explanation with a named site and at least two impacts.
Developing: some impacts identified but place detail thin.
Emerging: generic comments on tourism damage with no named example.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
‘Tourism does more harm than good in UK upland landscapes.’
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should give reasoned arguments to support and to oppose the statement and reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Footpath erosion at sites like Tarn Hows damages vegetation, soils and the visual landscape.
• Traffic congestion and air pollution accumulate on busy weekends, harming residents and wildlife.
• Second-home buying pushes house prices beyond local wages, hollowing out year-round communities.
• Honeypot pressure can overwhelm a single site’s carrying capacity in summer.

Arguments against:
• Tourism supports thousands of jobs in cafes, hotels, mountain rescue, transport and farm diversification.
• Visitor money funds path repair (Fix the Fells), ranger services and education programmes.
• National park designation, which protects the landscape, depends on tourism’s economic case.
• Visitor management strategies (park-and-ride, signage, zoning) can keep most pressure within carrying capacity.

Judgement: a balanced answer should weigh the cumulative damage at honeypot sites against the wider economic and protective benefits, ideally arguing that tourism is sustainable when managed but harmful when unmanaged.

Mastering: sustained evaluation with examples and a clear, supported conclusion.
Secure: clear arguments on both sides with named detail and a conclusion.
Developing: some arguments identified but conclusion weak or missing.
Emerging: simple list of points with no judgement.
[8 marks + 4 SPaG]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is true of an anticyclone?
A) Air rises and cools
B) Surface pressure is low
C) Air sinks and warms
D) Isobars are very tightly packed
practice_questions.marks: C) Air sinks and warms [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two characteristics of a depression.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark for each clear characteristic, up to 2:
• Low surface pressure / rising air (1).
• Cloud and rain associated with warm and cold fronts (1).
• Strong, gusty winds because isobars are closely spaced (1).
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a depression brings rain to the UK.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks for a clear cause-effect chain:
• Warm tropical air meets cold polar air at the polar front (1).
• The lighter warm air is forced to rise over the colder, denser air (1).
• As it rises it cools, water vapour condenses to form cloud, and rain falls (1).
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Compare the weather brought to the UK by a winter depression and a summer anticyclone.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Credit explicit comparison words:
• A winter depression brings rain, cloud and strong wind, whereas a summer anticyclone brings dry, settled and clear weather (1).
• Winter depressions are associated with low pressure (often below 990 mb), in contrast summer anticyclones have high pressure (often above 1,025 mb) (1).
• Depressions move quickly across the UK in 3–5 days, whereas anticyclones can stagnate for ten days or more (1).
• Both can produce hazards (storms vs heatwaves) — both have major economic impacts on transport and infrastructure (1).
[4 marks — must include explicit comparison links]

practice_questions.text: Using a named example, explain the consequences of one UK weather hazard caused by a depression.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks for a developed answer with locational detail:
• Names a specific event such as Storm Desmond (December 2015) or Storm Eunice (February 2022) (1).
• States a key statistic — Storm Desmond dropped 341 mm of rain on Honister Pass in 24 hours / Storm Eunice produced gusts of 196 km/h at the Needles (1).
• Describes a social consequence — about 5,200 homes flooded across Cumbria and Lancashire / three people killed in the UK during Eunice (1).
• Describes an economic consequence — insured losses estimated at £500m for Desmond / billions in damage and rail closures for Eunice (1).
• Describes an environmental consequence — soil washed off farmland, riverbanks collapsed, debris into rivers (1).
• Links the hazard to the depression: deep low pressure, warm and cold fronts producing prolonged rainfall and high winds (1).
[6 marks — locational detail and named example are essential]

practice_questions.text:
'Anticyclones cause more problems for the UK than depressions.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation comparing impacts of anticyclones (heatwaves, cold snaps, fog, drought) against depressions (storms, floods). Uses named examples (e.g. July 2022 heatwave, December 2010 cold snap, Storm Desmond, Storm Eunice) with numbers. Reaches a justified conclusion that recognises hazard type depends on season and location.

Secure: Clear arguments for and against, supported by at least one named example each side. Conclusion reached but partially asserted.

Developing: Some arguments on each side; examples generic ('a UK heatwave', 'a winter storm'). Limited weighing.

Emerging: Simple comments on weather hazards with no clear comparison and no examples.

In favour: 2022 heatwave linked to 3,000+ excess deaths, moorland fires, rail buckling; December 2010 blocking high gave the coldest UK December on record, −21.2°C at Altnaharra; long duration locks in problems.
Against: Storm Desmond — about 5,200 homes flooded across Cumbria and Lancashire, £500m insured losses; Storm Eunice — gusts of 196 km/h, three UK deaths, billions in damage; storms occur multiple times each winter.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes a hypothesis in a geographical enquiry?
A) A summary of secondary data collected from the internet
B) A testable prediction linking two variables that the fieldwork will check
C) A list of equipment needed for the fieldwork
D) A description of the data collection site
practice_questions.marks: B) A testable prediction linking two variables that the fieldwork will check [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways a geographer can collect primary data during fieldwork.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per valid descriptive point, up to 2 marks. Indicative content:
• Measuring physical variables (pebble long-axis with calipers, river width with a tape, gradient with a clinometer).
• Counting at fixed sites (pedestrian counts, traffic counts, vehicle types).
• Surveying opinions through printed questionnaires given to passers-by.
• Bi-polar environmental quality surveys scoring features 1 to 5.
• Taking annotated photos or field sketches of land use.
[2 marks — accept any two clearly described primary methods]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a geographer would use systematic sampling rather than opportunistic sampling on a beach pebble enquiry.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content:
• Systematic sampling takes pebbles at regular intervals (e.g. every 10 m) along the beach (1).
• This gives even coverage so the whole beach is represented, not just the easiest spots (1).
• Opportunistic sampling would tend to pick the largest or most colourful pebbles, biasing the results away from the true average size (1).
• Mastering: All three points connected with explicit cause-effect language and reference to bias and coverage.
• Secure: Two clear reasons; link to bias or representativeness present.
• Developing: One reason explained; second descriptive only.
• Emerging: Names methods but does not explain why one is better.
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Compare random and stratified sampling as ways of choosing where to take fieldwork measurements.
practice_questions.marks:
Two developed comparison points expected; explicit comparative language required. Indicative content:
• Both aim to reduce bias, but random sampling gives every site an equal chance of being picked, whereas stratified sampling first divides the area into groups and samples from each in proportion.
• Random sampling is quick to plan because it only needs random numbers, in contrast to stratified sampling which requires background information on the strata before fieldwork can begin.
• Both can produce representative results, but stratified sampling is better when the population is known to be uneven (e.g. land-use zones), whereas random sampling is better when the area is broadly uniform.
• A weakness shared by both is that they can still miss small but important features, similarly to systematic sampling.
• Mastering: Two developed compared points with explicit linking words and clear examples on each side.
• Secure: Two clear compared points with linking words.
• Developing: Compared points present but linking words missing or one side undeveloped.
• Emerging: Two parallel descriptions with no comparison.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Using a fieldwork example you have studied or planned, explain how a clear hypothesis improves the quality of a geographical enquiry.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content (any one well-developed example earns full marks):
• Example: 'Pebble long-axis decreases with distance from the headland because longshore drift sorts material as it moves.' This is testable because both variables (distance, pebble size) can be measured and compared.
• A clear hypothesis sets the variables, focuses the data collection sheet and tells the geographer exactly what equipment is needed (tape, calipers).
• It links the enquiry to a known process (longshore drift, sorting), so the conclusion can either support the existing geographical theory or challenge it.
• Without a hypothesis, fieldwork drifts into description and the enquiry cannot be evaluated against an expected outcome.
• A clear hypothesis also makes the enquiry replicable: another fieldworker could repeat it on a different beach and check whether the same relationship holds.
• Mastering: Sustained explanation with named context, specific variables and link to enquiry quality.
• Secure: Named example with two clear reasons a hypothesis improves enquiry quality.
• Developing: Named example but vague reasoning.
• Emerging: Generic example with no specific variables.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'A large sample size is the most important factor in producing reliable fieldwork results.' Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Larger samples reduce the influence of unusual single readings — a 50-respondent questionnaire reflects the population better than 10.
• More repeats per site (e.g. 10 width readings rather than 3) lower the impact of measurement error and reveal an average closer to the true value.
• Statistical techniques (mean, range, simple line of best fit) only become meaningful with enough data points.

Arguments against:
• Sampling method matters as much as size — 100 pebbles all picked opportunistically from the easiest spots produce a biased result, whereas 30 systematically sampled pebbles do not.
• Site choice matters: results from sites poorly placed for the question are unreliable however many readings are taken.
• Equipment accuracy and consistent technique are needed; tired fieldworkers misreading a clinometer add errors.
• Time and weather constraints mean huge samples are not always achievable; clear control of conditions can make a smaller sample more comparable.

Justified conclusion expected: sample size is necessary but not sufficient — reliability depends on size, method and conditions together.
• Mastering: Sophisticated argument with explicit judgement, two reasoned points each side, and place- or context-specific examples.
• Secure: Clear argument with two reasoned points each side and a justified conclusion.
• Developing: Some argument both sides; conclusion present but not justified.
• Emerging: One-sided list or no clear conclusion.
[8 marks plus SPaG]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes a volcanic hotspot?
A) A volcano that has erupted within the last twelve months
B) A localised plume of hot mantle that punches through a tectonic plate
C) A volcano that sits on a destructive plate boundary
D) A wide, gently sloping volcano made of basalt
practice_questions.marks: B) A localised plume of hot mantle that punches through a tectonic plate [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of a shield volcano.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for each feature described, up to two:
• Wide base and gently sloping sides because runny basaltic lava flows long distances before cooling.
• Built from many thin layers of fluid lava rather than ash.
• Often very large overall — Mauna Loa covers more than half of the Big Island of Hawaii.
• Found at constructive boundaries (Iceland) or hotspots (Hawaii) rather than at subduction zones.
• Eruptions are usually effusive (lava flows) rather than explosive.
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how convection currents in the mantle drive plate movement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Three linked points — heat from Earth's core warms mantle rock, which rises and spreads near the crust, cools and sinks back, and the resulting circular flow drags plates apart at constructive margins or together at destructive margins.
Secure: Two clear points explained with cause-effect.
Developing: Two points stated with limited explanation.
Emerging: One simple point.
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Compare a destructive plate boundary with a constructive plate boundary.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained comparison using linking words. Both boundary types covered with named examples (e.g. Pacific subduction at Mount St Helens vs Mid-Atlantic Ridge / Iceland) and contrasting features (subduction and trenches vs new ocean floor and rift valleys; explosive vs effusive eruptions).
Secure: Both boundaries described with relevant detail and clear comparison.
Developing: Two boundaries mentioned but described separately.
Emerging: One boundary described; little or no comparison.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Using a named example, explain how a volcanic hotspot creates a chain of islands.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A named hotspot (e.g. Hawaiian-Emperor chain) with specific evidence — Pacific Plate moving NW at about 7 cm/yr over a stationary plume, 5,800 km of islands, the Big Island sitting over the plume now while Kauai and Oahu have drifted past — linked to the resulting age progression and the future emergence of Lōʻihi.
Secure: Named hotspot with detail and at least two explained processes.
Developing: Some place-specific detail; one process explained.
Emerging: General reference to hotspots with no place-specific detail.
[6 marks — locational detail is essential]

practice_questions.text: 'Plate boundaries explain almost all volcanic activity on Earth.' Evaluate this statement. Reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Around 75% of the world's volcanoes sit on the Pacific Ring of Fire alone, all on plate boundaries.
• Subduction zones produce the most explosive volcanoes (Mount St Helens, Pinatubo).
• Constructive boundaries form the Mid-Atlantic Ridge — the longest volcanic feature on Earth.
• Explanation of plate boundaries covers most named volcanic landforms in the spec.

Arguments against:
• Volcanic hotspots like Hawaii and Yellowstone produce major volcanoes far from any plate boundary.
• The Hawaiian-Emperor chain stretches 5,800 km — clearly significant volcanic activity not driven by boundaries.
• Some hotspot eruptions (Yellowstone caldera) have been among the largest in geological history.
• Boundaries explain location, but not why some boundary volcanoes are explosive and others effusive — magma chemistry also matters.

Mastering: Sophisticated argument with both sides developed using named examples, weighted judgement and a justified conclusion.
Secure: Both sides argued with relevant evidence and a clear conclusion.
Developing: One side stronger; conclusion stated but limited justification.
Emerging: Simple points; little judgement.
[8 marks + 4 SPaG]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the UK's fertility rate in 2021?
A) Above the European average
B) Around 1.6 children per woman, below replacement level
C) Roughly equal to the death rate
D) Higher than in the 1960s
practice_questions.marks: B) Around 1.6 children per woman, below replacement level [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two consequences of an ageing UK population.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for each consequence described, up to two:
• Increased pressure on the NHS and adult social care because older people need more chronic and end-of-life care.
• Higher government spending on the state pension (around 10% of all government spending).
• Workforce shortages in nursing, teaching and engineering as people retire faster than they are replaced.
• A growing 'silver economy' as retirees spend on leisure, travel and home improvements.
• Concentration of older residents in coastal towns such as Eastbourne, supporting local services.
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why net migration into the UK is currently high.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Three linked reasons developed with cause-effect chains and named examples (e.g. EU work migration after 2004, humanitarian routes from Ukraine and Hong Kong, international students from South Asia).
Secure: Two clear reasons explained with cause-effect, at least one named example.
Developing: Two reasons stated with limited explanation, or one developed reason.
Emerging: One simple reason; little or no explanation.
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Compare the housing pressures faced by London with those faced by a rural area such as Pembrokeshire.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained comparison using linking words (whereas, in contrast, similarly). Both areas covered with specific detail — London's price-to-wage gap and high demand from young workers contrasted with Pembrokeshire's second-home market and locals priced out.
Secure: Clear comparison with linking words and relevant detail for both places.
Developing: Some comparison; tends to describe each place separately rather than link them.
Emerging: One place described; little or no comparison.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Using a UK example, explain how migration has changed the population of a city or town. Refer to specific places, numbers or features in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A named UK place (e.g. Boston in Lincolnshire, Leicester, Cardiff) with specific evidence — figures, source country, time period — and a clear chain explaining at least two consequences (e.g. demand for housing, pressure on schools, economic contribution, cultural change).
Secure: A named place with relevant detail and at least two explained consequences.
Developing: A named place with limited detail; one consequence explained.
Emerging: General reference to migration with no place-specific detail.
[6 marks — locational detail is essential]

practice_questions.text: 'Building 300,000 new homes a year is the only realistic answer to the UK's housing crisis.' Evaluate this statement. Reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• The shortfall between need (~300,000) and completions (~220,000) is the direct cause of unaffordable prices, especially in London and the south-east.
• A larger supply would slow price rises and let young adults move out of the family home.
• Brownfield development can deliver new homes without significant countryside loss.

Arguments against:
• The target alone does not control where homes are built; demand is concentrated and rural areas with second-home pressure may not benefit.
• Greenfield expansion meets resistance from local communities and damages habitats.
• Housing supply is one driver; affordability also depends on interest rates, wages and immigration policy.
• The shortage is partly a distribution problem — empty homes in northern towns sit alongside crowded southern markets.

Mastering: Sophisticated argument with both sides developed using named places, weighted judgement and a justified conclusion.
Secure: Both sides argued with relevant evidence and a clear conclusion.
Developing: One side stronger than the other; conclusion stated but limited justification.
Emerging: Simple points; little judgement.
[8 marks + 4 SPaG]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes a refugee?
A) A person who moves abroad for work and citizenship
B) A person forced to leave their country to escape war, persecution or disaster
C) A tourist on holiday in a foreign country
D) A person who returns home each year for cultural visits
practice_questions.marks: B) A person forced to leave their country to escape war, persecution or disaster [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe one cause of high infant mortality in sub-Saharan Africa.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: a clear cause with brief development, e.g. malnutrition leaves babies vulnerable to common infections that they cannot fight off; lack of clean water spreads diarrhoea, the third-biggest killer of under-fives. Secure: cause identified with limited development. Developing: vague reference to poverty. Emerging: no specific cause.

practice_questions.text: Explain why girls in many parts of sub-Saharan Africa do not complete secondary school.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: clear chain — school fees and uniform costs are out of reach for poorer families; long, unsafe walks to school deter parents; some girls leave for early marriage; lack of girls’ toilets pushes older girls out. Secure: one cause with brief explanation. Developing: states girls drop out without explanation. Emerging: no causal link.

practice_questions.text: Compare top-down and bottom-up approaches to tackling social challenges.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: explicit comparison using linking words on at least two points — both aim to improve quality of life, but top-down is large-scale and funded by governments or UN whereas bottom-up is small-scale and run with local communities; top-down can deliver mass vaccination quickly whereas bottom-up fits local culture and needs more closely. Secure: one explicit comparison. Developing: lists features separately. Emerging: only one feature named.

practice_questions.text: Explain how social challenges in sub-Saharan Africa or South Asia are being tackled. Use named examples.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: developed account with named country and named project (e.g. BRAC schools in Bangladesh, GAVI vaccines, India’s school meals scheme, UNHCR support for Rohingya at Cox’s Bazar) covering at least two challenges and how the project addresses them. Secure: named example with two challenges but limited detail. Developing: generic with one challenge. Emerging: vague reference without named place.

practice_questions.text:
“Education is the single most effective way to tackle social challenges in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia.”
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument with named examples weighing the case for education (girls’ schooling cuts child marriage and infant mortality, raises future income, BRAC Bangladesh) against alternatives (vaccination via GAVI, refugee support via UNHCR, conditional cash transfers cutting child labour, water and sanitation projects) reaching a justified judgement (e.g. education is the most powerful long-term lever but only when combined with health and refugee support). Secure: balanced argument with one named example. Developing: one-sided or generic. Emerging: simple agreement or disagreement without evidence.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best explains why western Britain is wetter than eastern Britain?
A) The east has higher mountains
B) The prevailing wind is from the south-west, dropping rain on western uplands
C) The east is closer to the Atlantic
D) The North Atlantic Drift cools the east coast
practice_questions.marks: B) The prevailing wind is from the south-west, dropping rain on western uplands [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe the climate of southern England.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for a developed description:
• Mild winters with average January temperatures around 5–6°C and warm summers averaging 18–20°C in July (1).
• Lower annual rainfall than the west (around 600 mm in the south-east) spread throughout the year (1).
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why temperatures in the Scottish Highlands are lower than those in southern England.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks for a clear cause-effect chain:
• The Highlands lie further north (around 57°N) so the sun's angle is lower, delivering less energy per square metre (1).
• They are at high altitude — temperature falls about 1°C per 100 m, so summits are 8–13°C cooler than valleys (1).
• They are exposed to cold polar maritime air masses arriving from the north-west, especially in winter (1).
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Compare the climate of western Scotland with that of eastern England.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Credit explicit comparison words:
• Western Scotland is wetter (over 3,000 mm/yr in the western Highlands) whereas eastern England is drier (Cambridge around 600 mm/yr) (1).
• Western Scotland is influenced by orographic uplift over mountains, in contrast eastern England sits in a rain shadow (1).
• Western Scotland has a stronger maritime influence and milder winters near the coast, whereas eastern England is more continental and feels colder in winter (1).
• Both areas can be very windy, but Scotland records more frequent storm-force gusts because of its position on the Atlantic seaboard (1).
[4 marks — must include explicit comparison links]

practice_questions.text: Using a named example, explain how human activity creates an urban heat island.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks for a developed answer with locational detail:
• Names a city, e.g. London (or Birmingham, Manchester) (1).
• Notes the size of the effect: 2°C warmer on average, 7°C warmer on still summer nights (1).
• Tarmac, brick and concrete absorb solar radiation by day and release it slowly at night, raising minimum temperatures (1).
• Vehicles, factories and air conditioning add waste heat to the air (1).
• Dense streets reduce wind speeds, preventing the city cooling by ventilation (1).
• Lack of vegetation means little evaporation, so less heat is removed by latent heat exchange (1).
[6 marks — locational detail and named example are essential]

practice_questions.text:
'The North Atlantic Drift is the most important factor shaping the UK's climate.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Use the StudyVault rubric.

Mastering: Sustained evaluation weighing the Drift against latitude, altitude, distance from the sea and prevailing wind. Uses named comparators (Plymouth vs Newfoundland; Seathwaite vs Cambridge; Ben Nevis vs Glen Nevis). Reaches a justified conclusion that the Drift is necessary but not sufficient — the UK's climate is the product of several factors interacting.

Secure: Clear arguments for and against. Some named places. Conclusion reached but partly asserted.

Developing: Some arguments on each side; examples generic. Limited weighing.

Emerging: Simple comments on the Drift; no comparison with other factors and no examples.

In favour: keeps west coast 5–9°C warmer in winter; reason ports remain ice-free; without it UK climate would resemble Newfoundland.
Against: prevailing south-westerly + relief explain rainfall split, not the Drift; latitude and altitude explain Highland cold; urban heat island shaped by human activity.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes a pyroclastic flow?
A) A slow-moving river of molten rock
B) A fast-moving current of hot gas, ash and rock at over 100 km/h
C) A mudflow of melted snow, ash and rock
D) A rising column of ash above a volcano
practice_questions.marks: B) A fast-moving current of hot gas, ash and rock at over 100 km/h [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two impacts of the 2010 Haiti earthquake.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for each impact described, up to two:
• Around 230,000 people killed by collapsing buildings.
• Roughly 300,000 people injured.
• About 250,000 homes destroyed or badly damaged, leaving more than a million homeless.
• Critical infrastructure including the main port and parts of central Port-au-Prince destroyed.
• Loss of police and government buildings hampered rescue and recovery.
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why volcanic monitoring is important for reducing the risk of eruptions.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Three linked points — instruments (seismometers, gas sensors, GPS) detect warning signs of an eruption days or weeks ahead; warnings allow timely evacuation; named example (Pinatubo 1991 — two months of monitoring led to around 60,000 people being evacuated before the eruption).
Secure: Two points clearly explained.
Developing: Two points stated with limited explanation.
Emerging: One point with little explanation.
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Compare the impacts of the 2010 Haiti earthquake with the 2011 Tōhoku earthquake.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained comparison using linking words (whereas, in contrast). Both events covered with named figures (Haiti M7.0, ~230,000 deaths; Tōhoku M9.0, ~18,500 deaths) and at least two contrasting reasons (building codes, income level, emergency services, warning systems).
Secure: Both events named with relevant detail; clear comparison.
Developing: Two events mentioned but described separately.
Emerging: One event described; little comparison.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Using a named example, explain how risk from a volcanic hazard has been reduced.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A named eruption (e.g. Mount Pinatubo 1991) with specific evidence — VEI 6, two months of monitoring by PHIVOLCS and USGS, evacuation of around 60,000 residents and 14,500 US Air Force personnel from Clark Air Base — linked to at least two reasons the death toll stayed at around 800 despite the eruption's size.
Secure: Named eruption with detail and at least two explained risk-reduction strategies.
Developing: Some place-specific detail; one strategy explained.
Emerging: General reference to risk reduction with no place-specific detail.
[6 marks — locational detail is essential]

practice_questions.text: 'It is human factors, not the size of the earthquake, that decide how many people die.' Evaluate this statement. Reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support (human factors decide):
• Tōhoku (M9.0) was over 1,000 times more powerful than Haiti (M7.0) but killed far fewer because of building codes, drills and warning systems.
• Pinatubo's VEI 6 eruption killed only ~800 because evacuation worked.
• Income, education and emergency services are stronger predictors of death tolls than magnitude.

Arguments against (physical factors still matter):
• Pyroclastic flows at 700°C are unsurvivable regardless of preparation — Saint-Pierre 1902 killed 28,000.
• A 14 m tsunami overtopped Japan's 5–10 m sea walls; some hazards exceed engineering limits.
• Very rural eruptions affect few people whatever the magnitude — exposure also depends on physical location.
• Magnitude does set the upper limit on possible damage.

Mastering: Sophisticated argument with both sides developed using named places, weighted judgement and a justified conclusion.
Secure: Both sides argued with relevant evidence and a clear conclusion.
Developing: One side stronger; conclusion stated but limited justification.
Emerging: Simple points; little judgement.
[8 marks + 4 SPaG]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following graph types is most suitable for showing the relationship between distance downstream and river width?
A) Pie chart
B) Choropleth map
C) Scatter graph
D) Population pyramid
practice_questions.marks: C) Scatter graph [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two reasons why a geographer might choose to calculate the median rather than the mean of a data set.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per valid descriptive point, up to 2 marks. Indicative content:
• The median ignores extreme values, so a single boulder does not distort the average pebble size.
• The median is the middle value when data is sorted, giving a fairer measure for skewed natural data.
• The mean is pulled towards extreme values, whereas the median is not, so the median better represents the typical value.
• The median is easier to calculate by hand for small samples and does not require summing all values.
[2 marks — accept any two distinct points]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a choropleth map is suitable for showing variations in deprivation by ward across a city.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content:
• Choropleth maps shade defined areas (wards) by value, so the city's overall pattern is visible at a glance (1).
• Darker shades for higher deprivation make the pattern easy for a non-specialist reader to follow (1).
• Wards are administrative areas with available data, so values can be compared like-for-like across the city (1).
• Mastering: Three connected points showing why the choropleth fits the spatial pattern.
• Secure: Two clear reasons; pattern visibility addressed.
• Developing: One reason; second descriptive only.
• Emerging: Names the map type but does not explain why it is suitable.
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Compare the inter-quartile range and the range as ways of describing the spread of fieldwork data.
practice_questions.marks:
Two developed comparison points expected; explicit comparative language required. Indicative content:
• Both measure how spread out the values are, but the range uses only the largest and smallest values, whereas the inter-quartile range uses only the middle 50% of values.
• The range is quick to calculate, in contrast to the IQR which needs the data sorted into quartiles before calculation.
• Both can be misleading if not interpreted carefully, but the range can be distorted by a single outlier, similarly to how the mean can be skewed by an extreme value.
• A key difference is that the IQR ignores outliers, whereas the range is dominated by them, so the IQR is more reliable for skewed natural data.
• Mastering: Two developed compared points with explicit linking words and clear examples.
• Secure: Two clear compared points with linking words.
• Developing: Compared points present but linking words missing or one side undeveloped.
• Emerging: Two parallel descriptions with no comparison.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Using a fieldwork example, explain how analysis can link the patterns shown by graphs to wider geographical theory.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content (any one developed example earns full marks):
• In a downstream river enquiry, scatter graphs of distance vs pebble size typically show a negative correlation. This fits the Bradshaw model: attrition wears pebbles smaller as they are transported downstream.
• Pedestrian flow surveys often show counts dropping with distance from the city centre. A line graph plotted across distance bands fits the bid-rent model, where peripheral shops attract fewer visitors than the central honeypot.
• In a hydrograph study, a steep rising limb after heavy rain indicates a flashy basin. Linking this to land use upstream (urbanisation, deforestation) connects the data to drainage-basin theory.
• In a coastal sediment study, decreasing pebble size with distance from a headland fits longshore-drift theory. Anomalies (a large pebble far from the headland) might be explained by recent cliff fall.
• Mastering: Sustained explanation with named context, specific theory and clear cause-effect link.
• Secure: Named example with clear theory link and a graph type.
• Developing: Named example but vague theory link.
• Emerging: Generic example with no theory link.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'A clear graph is more important than a careful statistical calculation when presenting fieldwork results.' Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• A well-chosen graph reveals the pattern at a glance — a scatter graph with a line of best fit is more accessible than a paragraph of summary numbers.
• Graphs let the reader spot anomalies and clusters quickly, which is harder to do from raw statistics.
• Spatial patterns in particular (choropleths, flow-line maps) cannot be conveyed by statistics alone — only by visual presentation.
• A confused graph (wrong type, missing axis labels) hides the pattern however correct the underlying numbers are.

Arguments against:
• Statistics let you compare strengths objectively — a small inter-quartile range proves the data is tightly clustered in a way the eye cannot judge from a graph.
• A line of best fit is only meaningful if the relationship is statistically real; without correlation analysis, a sketched line can mislead.
• Reporting just a graph without summary statistics (mean, IQR, percentage change) leaves the conclusion vague.
• Quoting specific figures from the data is expected, and that forces calculation rather than visual estimation.

Justified conclusion expected: graphs and statistics work together — graphs reveal patterns, statistics quantify them, and a strong analysis combines both.
• Mastering: Sophisticated argument with explicit judgement and two reasoned points each side.
• Secure: Clear argument with two reasoned points each side and a justified conclusion.
• Developing: Some argument both sides; conclusion present but not justified.
• Emerging: One-sided list or no clear conclusion.
[8 marks plus SPaG]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of fluvial transport by suspension?
A) A boulder being rolled along the bed
B) Pebbles bouncing along in short hops
C) Fine clay carried within the body of the water
D) Calcium carbonate dissolved in the water
practice_questions.marks: C) Fine clay carried within the body of the water [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two characteristics of a V-shaped valley.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Steep, sloping valley sides shaped by mass movement and weathering.
• A narrow valley floor with the river occupying most of it.
• A small, fast-flowing stream rather than a wide channel.
• Often found in the upper course of upland rivers.
[2 marks — 1 per characteristic]

practice_questions.text: Explain how hydraulic action contributes to the formation of a waterfall.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Water falling from the lip compresses air in cracks in the soft rock beneath.
• When the water moves on, the air expands suddenly, breaking off fragments of rock.
• Repeated cycles deepen the plunge pool and undercut the hard rock above, helping the waterfall retreat upstream.
[3 marks — 1 for a basic point, 2 for development, 3 for full process. Mastering: full cause-effect chain. Secure: clear explanation linked to the waterfall. Developing: one stage explained. Emerging: identifies hydraulic action only.]

practice_questions.text: Compare the dominant processes in the upper course and the lower course of a UK river.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Erosion in the upper course is mostly vertical, cutting downwards, whereas in the lower course it is mainly lateral on meander bends.
• Transport in the upper course is dominated by traction of boulders, in contrast to the lower course where suspension of fine silt is more important.
• Deposition is rare in the upper course because energy is high, whereas widespread floodplain deposition occurs in the lower course because energy is low.
• The upper course produces narrow features like V-shaped valleys; the lower course produces wide floodplains and oxbow lakes.
[4 marks — credit explicit comparison using ‘whereas’, ‘in contrast’, ‘similarly’.]

practice_questions.text: Using a named example, explain how meanders form along a UK river.
practice_questions.marks:
River Severn or River Wye are suitable. Students may include:
• A river such as the lower Severn flows across a gentle gradient, encouraging lateral erosion.
• Faster water on the outside of a slight bend erodes the bank by abrasion and hydraulic action, forming a river cliff.
• Slower water on the inner bend deposits sand and gravel as a slip-off slope.
• Over time the bends migrate sideways and downstream, exaggerating the meander.
• If the neck of a tight bend is cut through during a flood, an oxbow lake is left behind.

Mastering: developed explanation, named river, multiple linked processes.
Secure: clear sequence with named example.
Developing: process described but limited located detail.
Emerging: generic comments without a UK river named.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
‘Erosion is the most important process shaping UK river landscapes.’
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should give reasoned arguments to support and to oppose the statement, and reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Vertical erosion in upland courses produces the dramatic landforms students see first — V-shaped valleys, waterfalls and gorges.
• Lateral erosion creates meanders and the wide floodplains they sit in, shaping the lower course over centuries.
• Hydraulic action, abrasion, attrition and solution work continuously to break rock down.

Arguments against:
• Without transport, eroded material would pile up and stop the river working — saltation, suspension and traction move it on.
• Deposition is what produces the floodplains, levees and oxbow lakes that dominate UK lowlands.
• Rivers like the Severn near Shrewsbury are defined more by deposition than erosion in their lower course.
• All three processes work as a system; isolating one as ‘most important’ depends on which part of the course you study.

Judgement: a strong response argues that erosion drives the system at the top, but transport and deposition shape what students actually see in the lowlands. Importance is location-dependent.

Mastering: sustained evaluation with examples and clear conclusion.
Secure: clear arguments on both sides with examples.
Developing: some arguments but conclusion weak.
Emerging: list of points with no judgement.
[8 marks + 4 SPaG]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes a tariff?
A) A government payment given to local farmers
B) A tax placed on goods imported from another country
C) A limit on how many goods can be imported
D) A free-trade agreement between countries
practice_questions.marks: B) A tax placed on goods imported from another country [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of enclave tourism.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: a clear feature with brief development, e.g. visitors stay inside a self-contained resort owned by a foreign company, so little of what they spend reaches the local economy. Secure: feature identified with limited development. Developing: vague reference to tourism only benefiting some people. Emerging: no feature identified or definition restated.

practice_questions.text: Explain how trade rules can hold back development in LICs.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: clear cause-and-effect chain with two examples — tariffs raise the price of LIC exports in HIC markets, reducing demand; subsidies make HIC products artificially cheap, undercutting LIC producers; quotas cap how much LICs can sell. Secure: one mechanism with effect. Developing: states trade is unfair without explanation. Emerging: no link to development.

practice_questions.text: Compare the impact of MNCs and tourism as drivers of development in lower-income countries.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: explicit comparison using linking words (similarly, whereas, in contrast) on at least two points — both create jobs, but MNC jobs are factory-based whereas tourism jobs are service-based; both bring foreign money in, however MNC profits often leave the country whereas tourism revenue can flow more directly into local services if non-enclave. Secure: one explicit comparison. Developing: lists features of each separately. Emerging: only one feature named.

practice_questions.text: Explain how multinational companies have affected development in one named LIC or NIC. Use named examples.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: developed account with named country (e.g. Bangladesh, Vietnam, Mexico) and named MNC or industry (e.g. garment industry employing four million workers; Foxconn assembling Apple products in Vietnam) covering at least two impacts — jobs, training, infrastructure, tax revenue against low wages, profit repatriation, sudden closures. Secure: named country with two impacts but limited locational detail. Developing: generic LIC reference, one impact. Emerging: vague reference without named place.

practice_questions.text:
“Tourism does more harm than good for the development of LICs and NICs.”
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument with named examples (e.g. Kenya, Thailand, Maldives) weighing benefits (employment, foreign currency, infrastructure such as roads and airports, multiplier effects) against costs (enclave resorts limiting local income, cultural change, environmental pressure, vulnerability to political shocks) and reaching a justified judgement (e.g. tourism is a net positive when local ownership is encouraged but harmful when it stays in foreign-owned enclaves). Secure: balanced argument with one named example and a clear conclusion. Developing: one-sided argument or generic without named places. Emerging: simple agreement or disagreement without evidence.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes reliability in a fieldwork enquiry?
A) How close a measurement is to the true value
B) Whether the same method would produce similar results if repeated
C) Whether the data supports the hypothesis
D) The size of the sample taken at each site
practice_questions.marks: B) Whether the same method would produce similar results if repeated [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways a fieldwork enquiry could be biased.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per valid descriptive point, up to 2 marks. Indicative content:
• Surveying shoppers only on a sunny weekend gives an unrepresentative picture of the high street.
• A questionnaire with leading questions pushes respondents towards particular answers.
• Choosing accessible sites only (skipping muddy or steep ground) misses parts of the study area.
• Using secondary data from a single source, such as a tourist board, may emphasise positive findings.
• Recording readings only at one time of day overlooks daily variation in pedestrian or traffic flow.
[2 marks — accept any two distinct points]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a conclusion that quotes specific figures is stronger than one that says 'the data supports the hypothesis'.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content:
• Quoting specific figures shows the conclusion is grounded in your own evidence rather than a general impression (1).
• Figures let the reader see the size of the change and judge whether the pattern is strong or weak (1).
• Specific evidence makes the conclusion easier to test against geographical theory and to compare with other studies (1).
• Mastering: Three connected points showing why specific evidence raises conclusion quality.
• Secure: Two clear reasons.
• Developing: One reason explained; second descriptive only.
• Emerging: Generic comment without addressing why figures help.
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Compare reliability and accuracy in fieldwork.
practice_questions.marks:
Two developed comparison points expected; explicit comparative language required. Indicative content:
• Both relate to the quality of measurements, but accuracy is how close a single reading is to the true value, whereas reliability is how consistent results are when the method is repeated.
• A clinometer used by a trained student can be accurate, in contrast to the same clinometer used by an untrained classmate which is less reliable.
• Both are needed for a trustworthy enquiry, similarly to the way valid sampling and large sample size are both needed.
• A method can be reliable without being accurate (consistently wrong) or accurate without being reliable (right once but variable), so they must be considered separately.
• Mastering: Two developed compared points with explicit linking words and clear examples.
• Secure: Two clear compared points with linking words.
• Developing: Compared points present but linking words missing.
• Emerging: Two parallel descriptions with no comparison.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Using a fieldwork example, explain how realistic improvements to methods can strengthen a future enquiry.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content (any one developed example earns full marks):
• In a Welsh river enquiry, repeating measurements at three depths per cross-section rather than one would average out turbulence and give a more reliable picture of channel shape.
• A high-street pedestrian-flow study could be repeated on a weekday and a weekend at three times of day to capture daily and weekly variation.
• A coastal pebble study could include both Welsh and English beach sites to test whether the longshore-drift pattern holds in contrasting environments.
• A questionnaire could be redesigned to remove leading questions and use closed-question formats, making the data easier to compare across respondents.
• A clinometer survey could pair every reading between two students to flag and re-measure any disagreement, raising reliability.
• Mastering: Sustained explanation with named context, specific change and clear cause-effect link to enquiry quality.
• Secure: Named example with two clear improvements.
• Developing: Named example but vague improvements ('take more readings').
• Emerging: Generic improvements with no specific context.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'When making a UK decision, expert opinion should always be valued more than local people's views.' Evaluate this statement using examples of UK decision-making you have studied.
In your answer you should:
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Experts have detailed evidence — coastal engineers can model erosion rates, hydrologists can predict flood return periods, ecologists can assess biodiversity loss.
• Without expert input, decisions on coastal management or wind farm siting risk costly mistakes that local opinion alone cannot prevent.
• Long-term consequences (climate change, sea-level rise, biodiversity collapse) sit outside daily local experience and need specialist evidence.
• Cost-benefit analysis depends on technical data only experts can provide.

Arguments against:
• Local people understand the day-to-day reality of a place — recent flood patterns, tourist pressure, livelihoods, sense of community.
• Expert reports can miss social or cultural costs (homes lost to managed retreat, communities split by infrastructure).
• Local knowledge has been shown to add to expert work, for example fishing communities flagging changes in coastal sediment patterns earlier than monitoring stations.
• Decisions imposed without local consent often face resistance, delaying or derailing the project.

Justified conclusion expected: a balanced decision listens to both — experts for the long-term technical evidence, locals for lived experience and acceptance of the outcome. Either alone produces unbalanced decisions.
• Mastering: Sophisticated argument with explicit judgement, named UK examples and weighing of evidence.
• Secure: Clear argument with two reasoned points each side and a justified conclusion.
• Developing: Some argument both sides; conclusion present but not justified.
• Emerging: One-sided list or no clear conclusion.
[8 marks plus SPaG]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best defines emergency aid?
A) Long-term aid that builds schools and clinics over many years
B) Short-term aid given immediately after a disaster
C) A loan from one government to another with conditions
D) The community premium paid to fair trade farmers
practice_questions.marks: B) Short-term aid given immediately after a disaster [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of long-term development aid.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: a clear feature with brief development, e.g. it funds lasting projects such as schools, clinics, water supplies or training, building local capacity over many years. Secure: feature identified with limited development. Developing: vague reference to helping poor countries. Emerging: no feature identified.

practice_questions.text: Explain how fair trade benefits producers in low-income countries.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: clear chain — a guaranteed minimum price protects farmers from world price crashes; a community premium funds schools or clinics; producers gain a more stable income they can plan around. Secure: one mechanism with effect. Developing: states fair trade is good without explanation. Emerging: no link to producers.

practice_questions.text: Compare emergency aid and long-term development aid.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: explicit comparison with linking words on at least two points — both transfer money or goods to recipient countries, but emergency aid lasts days or weeks whereas long-term aid runs for years; emergency aid responds to disasters whereas long-term aid builds schools, clinics and water supplies. Secure: one explicit comparison. Developing: lists features of each separately without comparing. Emerging: only one feature named.

practice_questions.text: Explain how NGOs and aid can help close the development gap. Use named examples.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: developed account with named NGO or aid project (e.g. WaterAid hand-pump wells in Malawi, Oxfam education projects, UN response to Haiti 2010 earthquake) covering at least two impacts — lives saved, school enrolment, access to clean water, health improvements. Secure: named example with two impacts but limited detail. Developing: generic NGO reference with one impact. Emerging: vague reference without named examples.

practice_questions.text:
“Aid does more harm than good for poorer countries.”
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument with named examples weighing benefits (lives saved by emergency aid, schools and clinics built by long-term aid, multiplier effects on local economies) against costs (corruption losses, tied aid undercutting local firms, dependency, poor projects that ignore local needs) and reaching a justified judgement (e.g. aid is most effective when paired with NGO bottom-up work and recipient-government oversight). Secure: balanced argument with one named example and clear conclusion. Developing: one-sided or generic. Emerging: simple agreement or disagreement without evidence.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best defines food miles?
A) The total carbon released in growing a food product
B) The distance food travels from where it is produced to where it is consumed
C) The shelf life of a food once packaged
D) The price difference between local and imported food
practice_questions.marks: B) The distance food travels from where it is produced to where it is consumed [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe one impact of e-waste on the environment.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: a clear impact with brief development, e.g. burning electronics to extract copper releases toxic chemicals like lead and mercury into soil and air, harming local communities. Secure: impact identified with limited development. Developing: vague reference to pollution. Emerging: no specific impact.

practice_questions.text: Explain why ecological footprints are larger in HICs than in LICs.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: clear chain — HIC residents earn more so eat more meat, fly more, drive more and buy more electronics; each activity uses more land, water and energy; cheaper imports raise consumption further. Secure: one mechanism with effect. Developing: states richer countries use more resources without explaining. Emerging: no causal link.

practice_questions.text: Compare food miles and full carbon footprint as measures of food's environmental impact.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: explicit comparison using linking words on at least two points — both try to capture environmental impact, however food miles count only the distance whereas full carbon footprint includes growing, refrigeration and energy; food miles can mislead (a heated UK greenhouse tomato may have a bigger footprint than one shipped chilled from Spain) whereas full carbon footprint gives a fairer picture. Secure: one explicit comparison. Developing: lists features separately. Emerging: only one feature named.

practice_questions.text: Explain how consumerism in HICs has changed environments in LICs and NICs. Use named examples.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: developed account with named products and places (e.g. palm oil clearance in Indonesia/Malaysia for biscuits and soap, Agbogbloshie e-waste site in Ghana, Brazilian beef driving Amazon clearance, food miles for Kenyan cut flowers and out-of-season strawberries) covering at least two impacts — deforestation, soil degradation, carbon emissions, toxic pollution. Secure: named example with two impacts but limited detail. Developing: generic with one impact. Emerging: vague reference without named place.

practice_questions.text:
“Reducing consumerism is the most important way to protect the global environment.”
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument with named examples weighing strengths of cutting consumption (lower food miles, less palm oil clearance in Indonesia, less e-waste at Agbogbloshie, lower greenhouse gas emissions) against alternatives (technology-driven solutions like renewable energy, government-led policy like carbon taxes and right-to-repair laws, international agreements like the Paris Agreement) and reaching a justified judgement (e.g. cutting consumption is essential but only laws and global agreements deliver change at scale). Secure: balanced argument with one named example. Developing: one-sided or generic. Emerging: simple agreement or disagreement without evidence.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes coastal flooding?
A) The slow weathering of cliff faces by rain
B) The temporary submerging of coastal land when seawater is driven inland
C) The deposition of sand to form new beaches
D) The drying out of salt marsh during low tide
practice_questions.marks: B) The temporary submerging of coastal land when seawater is driven inland [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two physical factors that increase coastal vulnerability.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for each factor described, up to two:
• Soft rock geology — clay or glacial till erodes far faster than granite or limestone.
• Low-lying coastal shape — flat coasts have no high ground to break a storm surge.
• Long fetch — open sea allows waves to build up power before reaching the shore.
• Frequent or severe storms produce larger waves and storm surges.
• Climate change — sea level rise and stronger storms together multiply risk.
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why climate change is increasing the risk to coastal communities.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Three linked points — thermal expansion of warmer seas raises levels; melting glaciers and polar ice add to ocean volume; warmer seas fuel stronger storms that breach existing defences; outcome is more frequent flooding even where defences exist.
Secure: Two points clearly explained.
Developing: Two points stated with limited explanation.
Emerging: One point with little explanation.
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Compare the vulnerability of the Maldives with that of the Netherlands.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained comparison using linking words. Both countries covered with named detail (Maldives 1.5 m average elevation, GNI ~US$13,000; Netherlands 17 million people, €1 billion/yr Delta Works) and a clear contrast that physical vulnerability is similar but economic capacity is very different.
Secure: Both countries named with relevant detail; clear comparison.
Developing: Two countries mentioned but described separately.
Emerging: One country described; little or no comparison.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Using a named UK example, explain why one coastline is more vulnerable to erosion than others.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A named UK coastline (e.g. Holderness, East Yorkshire) with specific evidence — glacial till cliffs, 1.8 m/yr retreat, at least 23 villages lost since Roman times, defences at Mappleton causing increased erosion at Great Cowden of up to 10 m/yr — linked to at least two reasons (soft geology, long fetch, knock-on effects of defences).
Secure: Named coast with detail and at least two explained reasons.
Developing: Some place-specific detail; one reason explained.
Emerging: General reference to coastal erosion with no place-specific detail.
[6 marks — locational detail is essential]

practice_questions.text: 'Wealth is more important than geography in deciding which coastal communities suffer most from sea level rise.' Evaluate this statement. Reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support (wealth is more important):
• The Netherlands and the Maldives are both extremely low-lying, but only the Netherlands can fund €1 billion a year of defences.
• Bangladesh's 14,000 cyclone shelters and 12,000 km of embankments cut Cyclone Amphan deaths to 26 — wealth and planning replaced loss of life.
• Wealthy nations can afford insurance, recovery and managed retreat.

Arguments against (geography is decisive):
• Some islands and atolls have no high ground to retreat to whatever their wealth (Maldives 1.5 m mean elevation).
• Soft geology like Holderness clay erodes regardless of how much money is spent — Mappleton's defences just shifted the problem to Great Cowden.
• Storm tracks and fetch are physical givens — the 1953 North Sea storm surge overwhelmed defences in both England (~307 deaths) and the Netherlands (~1,800 deaths).
• Climate change adds physical risk faster than even the richest countries can adapt.

Mastering: Sophisticated argument with both sides developed using named places and figures, weighted judgement and a justified conclusion.
