Secure: Both sides argued with relevant evidence and a clear conclusion.
Developing: One side stronger; conclusion stated but limited justification.
Emerging: Simple points; little judgement.
[8 marks + 4 SPaG]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes a brownfield site?
A) Open countryside used for grazing
B) Land that has been previously built on, often industrial or derelict
C) Protected land in a National Park
D) A new housing estate on farmland
practice_questions.marks: B) Land that has been previously built on, often industrial or derelict [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Egan's wheel.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for each feature described, up to two:
• Eight spokes/components covering governance, transport, services, environment, economy, housing, social and cultural life, and equity.
• A diagram used by UK planners since 2004 to test whether new developments will be sustainable.
• Each spoke must be present for a community to be considered sustainable, not just one or two.
• Created by Sir John Egan in a 2004 government review.
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why brownfield development is often preferred over greenfield in UK planning policy.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Three linked reasons (e.g. protects countryside / green belt; uses existing infrastructure cutting emissions and costs; revives deprived neighbourhoods) developed with cause-effect.
Secure: Two reasons clearly explained.
Developing: Two reasons stated with limited explanation.
Emerging: One reason with little or no explanation.
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Compare a brownfield development you have studied with a greenfield development you have studied.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained comparison using linking words (whereas, in contrast). Both case studies named (e.g. Cardiff Bay vs Northstowe) with specific evidence — 6,000 homes/25,000 jobs at Cardiff Bay vs 10,000 homes/30% affordable at Northstowe — and judgement about strengths and weaknesses.
Secure: Both places named with relevant detail; clear comparison.
Developing: Two places mentioned but described separately rather than compared.
Emerging: One place described; little or no comparison.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Using a named UK example, explain how a brownfield site has been regenerated to create a more sustainable community.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A named brownfield case study (e.g. Cardiff Bay) with specific evidence — barrage built 1999, 200-hectare lake, 6,000 homes, 25,000 jobs, Wales Millennium Centre 2004 — linked to at least three spokes of Egan's wheel (e.g. economy, services, transport).
Secure: Named case study with detail and at least two explained sustainability gains.
Developing: Some place-specific detail; one sustainability point made.
Emerging: General reference to brownfield with no place-specific detail.
[6 marks — locational detail is essential]

practice_questions.text: 'New homes in the UK should be built on greenfield land rather than brownfield.' Evaluate this statement. Reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support of greenfield:
• Greenfield sites can deliver large planned new towns (e.g. Northstowe — 10,000 homes, bus rapid-transit corridor) that include schools, shops and transport from the start.
• Building costs are lower because there is no contamination to clean up.
• Modern masterplans can include affordable housing (30% at Northstowe) and renewable energy.

Arguments against:
• Brownfield reuse protects countryside and the green belt; consumes no farmland.
• Cardiff Bay shows brownfield can deliver 6,000 homes plus 25,000 jobs in an existing transport network.
• Greenfield can lock in car dependency and lengthen commutes if poorly planned.
• Both should be assessed against Egan's wheel — neither is automatically sustainable.

Mastering: Sophisticated argument with both sides developed using named case studies, weighted judgement and a justified conclusion using Egan's wheel.
Secure: Both sides argued with relevant evidence and a clear conclusion.
Developing: One side stronger; conclusion stated but limited justification.
Emerging: Simple points; little judgement.
[8 marks + 4 SPaG]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the largest scale of ecosystem?
A) Pond
B) Hedgerow
C) Biome
D) Forest floor
practice_questions.marks: C) Biome [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two characteristics of the tropical rainforest climate.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark for each developed characteristic, up to 2:
• Average temperatures of around 25–30°C all year, with little seasonal variation (1).
• Heavy annual rainfall, often exceeding 2,000 mm, distributed throughout the year (1).
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why tropical rainforest soils become infertile when the trees are cleared.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks for a clear cause-effect chain:
• Most nutrients in a rainforest are stored in the living biomass (the trees), not the soil (1).
• When trees are cut down, the rapid cycle between leaf fall, decomposition and tree roots is broken (1).
• Heavy rainfall then leaches the few remaining nutrients out of the thin soil, leaving it too poor for crops within a few years (1).
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Compare a tropical rainforest and a UK hedgerow as ecosystems.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Credit explicit comparison words:
• A tropical rainforest is a global-scale biome covering millions of km², whereas a UK hedgerow is a small-scale ecosystem just a few metres wide (1).
• The rainforest has high biodiversity (50% of world species in 6% of land), in contrast a hedgerow's biodiversity is more modest but very high per metre for the UK (1).
• Both have a layered structure (emergents/canopy in rainforest; canopy/shrubs/ground in hedgerow), supporting different species at each level (1).
• The rainforest has poor soils with rapid nutrient cycling; in contrast hedgerow soils are deeper and richer because temperate decomposition is slower (1).
[4 marks — must include explicit comparison links]

practice_questions.text: Using a named example, explain how plants are adapted to live in the tropical rainforest.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks for a developed answer with locational and biological detail:
• Names the tropical rainforest (e.g. the Amazon basin) (1).
• Identifies a specific plant adaptation: buttress roots up to 5 m tall (1).
• Explains its purpose: support enormous trunks in shallow rainforest soil (1).
• Identifies a second adaptation: drip-tip leaves (1).
• Explains its purpose: shed heavy rainfall quickly to prevent fungal growth (1).
• Adds a third adaptation: lianas climb existing trees to reach canopy light without growing thick trunks (1).
[6 marks — locational detail and at least two distinct adaptations are essential]

practice_questions.text:
'Small-scale UK ecosystems are more important to protect than large global biomes.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Use the StudyVault rubric.

Mastering: Sustained evaluation comparing the value of UK hedgerows (or another small-scale ecosystem) with that of tropical rainforest. Uses named statistics (2,100+ hedgerow species, £500m crop pollination; 50% world species in rainforest; deforestation rates). Reaches a justified conclusion (e.g. both are important but at different scales; loss of large biomes affects global climate, loss of UK hedgerows affects local biodiversity).

Secure: Clear arguments for and against. Some named examples. Conclusion partly asserted.

Developing: Some arguments on each side; examples generic. Limited weighing.

Emerging: Simple comments on ecosystems with no comparison and no examples.

In favour of UK ecosystems: easier for UK governments to protect; provide direct services to UK food production; under-funded; protected by local laws.
Against (favour global biomes): rainforests store far more carbon and biodiversity; their loss has global climate consequences; UK ecosystem health depends on global stability.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes longshore drift?
A) Rocks falling vertically off a cliff
B) Sediment moving along the coast in a zig-zag pattern
C) Waves cutting a notch into a cliff base
D) Sand being blown inland by the wind
practice_questions.marks: B) Sediment moving along the coast in a zig-zag pattern [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of a wave-cut platform.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• A flat or gently sloping rocky surface at the foot of a cliff.
• Exposed only at low tide, often covered with rock pools and seaweed.
• Marks the line of cliff retreat over hundreds or thousands of years.
• Typically built into rocks of moderate resistance such as limestone or sandstone.
[2 marks — 1 per feature]

practice_questions.text: Explain how a stack forms.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Hydraulic action and abrasion widen cracks in a headland into caves.
• Caves on opposite sides of a headland meet to form an arch.
• Continued erosion thins the arch until it collapses, leaving a stack standing offshore.
[3 marks — 1 simple, 2 development, 3 full sequence. Mastering: clear cause-effect through three stages. Secure: identifies arch and stack with a process. Developing: one stage. Emerging: terms only.]

practice_questions.text: Compare the formation of headlands and bays with the formation of spits.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Headlands and bays form by erosion of rocks of different resistance, whereas spits form by deposition of sediment moved by longshore drift.
• Headlands and bays develop where rock bands meet the sea at right angles; in contrast, spits form where the coast bends sharply or an estuary opens.
• The dominant processes differ — hydraulic action and abrasion shape headlands and bays, whereas deposition in low-energy water shapes spits.
• Both depend on the supply of sediment, but headlands lose it while spits gain it.
[4 marks — credit explicit comparison.]

practice_questions.text: Using a named UK example, explain how a spit forms.
practice_questions.marks:
Spurn Head (Yorkshire) is suitable. Students may include:
• Sediment from the rapidly eroding boulder clay cliffs of Holderness travels south along the coast by longshore drift in a south-easterly direction.
• When the coast turns sharply west into the Humber estuary, the wave energy drops and sand and shingle are deposited.
• Material accumulates as a long, narrow ridge curving into the estuary — Spurn Head is around 5 km long.
• A change in wind direction occasionally curves the end landwards into a hooked recurve.
• Behind the spit, sheltered water allows mudflats and salt marsh to develop, supporting migrating birds.

Mastering: developed explanation, named place, multiple linked processes.
Secure: clear sequence with example.
Developing: process described but located detail thin.
Emerging: generic answer with no UK example.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
‘Erosional landforms tell us more about a coast than depositional ones.’
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Cliffs, stacks and headlands reveal rock type, resistance and structure (e.g. Old Harry Rocks shows chalk weakness).
• Erosion rates record long-term storm frequency and the energy environment of the coast.
• Without erosion there would be no sediment for deposition further down-drift.

Arguments against:
• Spits, beaches and bars record longshore drift direction and supply, telling us where and how sediment moves.
• Salt marshes behind spits indicate sheltered, low-energy environments and biological richness.
• Patterns of deposition (e.g. recurves, lagoons) show changes in wind, sea level and human management.
• Both erosion and deposition are needed for a full picture.

Judgement: a strong answer argues that erosion and deposition are complementary — each tells half the story; together they explain the whole sediment budget of a coast.

Mastering: sustained evaluation, named coasts, clear judgement.
Secure: arguments on both sides with examples.
Developing: imbalanced or weak conclusion.
Emerging: list without judgement.
[8 marks + 4 SPaG]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes ecotourism?
A) Mass tourism in coastal resorts with all-inclusive hotels
B) Small-scale tourism in fragile environments where most income stays local and supports conservation
C) Cruise tourism that visits multiple countries in one trip
D) Domestic tourism within a tourist's own country only
practice_questions.marks: B) Small-scale tourism in fragile environments where most income stays local and supports conservation [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways tourism can damage coral reefs.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per valid descriptive point, up to 2 marks. Indicative content:
• Snorkellers and reef-walkers physically break corals by touching or standing on them.
• Boat anchors dropped onto reef break the coral structure.
• Sunscreen chemicals in the water cause coral bleaching.
• Hotel construction on mangrove coastlines removes natural buffers and increases sediment runoff.
• Overfishing or fish-feeding by tour operators disturbs reef food webs.
[2 marks — accept any two distinct points clearly described]

practice_questions.text: Explain how wetland restoration can reduce flood risk for towns downstream.
practice_questions.marks:
Mark for a clear cause-effect chain. Indicative content:
• Restored wetlands store water during heavy rainfall instead of letting it run straight to the river (1).
• This slows the rate at which water reaches downstream channels, lowering peak discharge (1).
• A lower peak discharge means river levels stay below flood-defence height in towns downstream (1).
• Mastering: Sophisticated cause-effect chain with explicit reference to lag time, peak discharge or storage capacity.
• Secure: Clear three-step explanation linking storage to reduced flood risk.
• Developing: Two-step explanation; some link missing.
• Emerging: One simple point or pure description with no causal link.
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Compare wetland restoration in the UK with ecotourism in a tropical environment as ways of managing habitats.
practice_questions.marks:
Two developed comparison points needed; explicit comparative language ('whereas', 'in contrast', 'similarly') expected. Indicative content:
• Both aim to protect biodiversity, but wetland restoration in the UK rebuilds a damaged habitat, whereas ecotourism in the tropics uses visitor income to maintain a habitat that is still largely intact.
• Wetland restoration is funded by government schemes such as agri-environment payments, in contrast to ecotourism which is funded directly by tourist spending and park fees.
• Both bring economic benefits to local people; UK restoration pays farmers to manage wetter land, similarly tropical ecotourism employs local guides and lodge staff.
• A key difference is scale of visitor pressure: UK restored fens have low visitor numbers, whereas tropical reefs and rainforests must cap tourists to avoid damaging the habitat they depend on.
• Mastering: Two developed compared points with explicit linking words and named examples on both sides.
• Secure: Two clear compared points with linking words; examples present.
• Developing: Compared points present but linking words missing or one side undeveloped.
• Emerging: Two parallel descriptions with no comparison.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Using a named example, explain how ecotourism can help protect a fragile habitat.
practice_questions.marks:
Reward depth, accuracy and specificity. Indicative content (any one well-developed example is sufficient for full marks):
• Costa Rica protects roughly a quarter of its land area; national park fees pay for rangers, replanting and species monitoring, so visitor numbers directly fund conservation.
• In Sabah, Malaysian Borneo, ecotourism lodges along the Kinabatangan River employ local people as guides and trackers — villagers earn more from intact rainforest than from selling land for palm oil, so the forest is conserved.
• Lodges in Borneo cap visitor numbers per boat trip and use solar power and on-site wastewater treatment, reducing the environmental footprint of tourism on the rainforest.
• In Belize, cruise-ship passenger fees fund monitoring of the barrier reef, helping to detect bleaching and overfishing early.
• Mastering: Sustained explanation with named place, specific figures or named species, and clear cause-effect link to habitat protection.
• Secure: Named example with two clear ways tourism protects the habitat.
• Developing: Named example but vague mechanisms.
• Emerging: Generic 'African country' or 'tropical island' with no specific detail.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'Restoring damaged habitats is more important than promoting ecotourism.' Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support of the statement:
• Restoration tackles damage that has already happened — once species are lost or peat dries out, ecotourism alone cannot bring them back.
• Wetland restoration provides ecosystem services beyond biodiversity (flood storage, carbon capture) that benefit everyone, not just visitors.
• Restoration projects like the Great Fen pay farmers fairly through agri-environment schemes, providing reliable, long-term funding rather than tourism revenue which can collapse during recessions or pandemics.
• Many tropical habitats are too fragile for any tourism — restoration may be the only viable option.

Arguments against the statement:
• Ecotourism funds restoration directly. Costa Rica's national park fees and Belize's cruise-ship tax pay for replanting, ranger patrols and reef monitoring.
• Without ecotourism revenue, communities in places like Borneo would have stronger economic reasons to clear forests for palm oil.
• Restoration alone cannot keep habitats intact long-term if local people see no economic benefit; ecotourism gives nature a value that competes with extractive industries.
• Many habitats (intact rainforest, healthy reefs) need maintenance not restoration — ecotourism is the right tool there.

Justified conclusion expected. Indicative judgement: both are needed and work best together — restoration repairs damage, ecotourism creates the income and political support to keep restored habitats protected.
• Mastering: Sophisticated argument with explicit judgement, named examples on both sides, and weighing of evidence.
• Secure: Clear argument with two reasoned points each side and a justified conclusion.
• Developing: Some argument both sides; conclusion present but not justified.
• Emerging: One-sided list or no clear conclusion.
[8 marks plus SPaG]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best defines water security?
A) The total amount of rainfall a country receives in a year
B) Reliable access to enough safe water to meet a population's needs
C) The percentage of water used for agriculture in a country
D) The cost of water transferred between regions
practice_questions.marks: B) Reliable access to enough safe water to meet a population's needs [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of a water transfer scheme.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: a clear feature with brief development, e.g. water is moved long distances by canal or pipeline from a wet region to a dry one, often using pumping stations and energy. Secure: feature identified with limited development. Developing: vague reference to moving water. Emerging: no feature identified.

practice_questions.text: Explain why global demand for water is rising.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: a clear chain — rising population means more people drinking, washing and farming; richer diets demand more meat and dairy, which take far more water to produce per kilo; intensive farming and industry use more water per person than traditional methods. Secure: one mechanism with brief explanation. Developing: states demand is rising without explanation. Emerging: no link to development or population.

practice_questions.text: Compare large dams and rainwater harvesting as ways of managing water supply.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: explicit comparison using linking words on at least two points — both increase reliable water supply, but dams operate at national or regional scale whereas rainwater harvesting operates at household scale; dams generate hydro-electricity whereas rainwater harvesting does not; dams flood land and displace people whereas rainwater harvesting rarely causes social impacts. Secure: one explicit comparison. Developing: lists features separately. Emerging: only one feature named.

practice_questions.text: Explain how water resources are managed in one named country or region. Use named examples.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: developed account with named country or scheme (e.g. China and the Three Gorges Dam, Ghana and the Akosombo Dam, India and rainwater harvesting, China’s South-North Water Transfer) covering at least two strategies and their consequences (irrigation, hydro-electricity, displacement, sediment loss). Secure: named example with two strategies but limited locational detail. Developing: generic with one strategy. Emerging: vague reference without named place.

practice_questions.text:
“Large dams are the best way to manage water resources in low- and middle-income countries.”
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument with named examples weighing benefits of dams (year-round water, irrigation, hydro-electricity, flood control, e.g. Three Gorges, Akosombo) against costs (population displacement, lost farmland, sediment loss, ecological damage, earthquake risk) and against alternatives (rainwater harvesting, drip irrigation, leak repair, water transfers) reaching a justified judgement (e.g. dams suit large populations and reliable rivers but small-scale appropriate technology fits remote rural areas better). Secure: balanced argument with one named example. Developing: one-sided or generic. Emerging: simple agreement or disagreement without evidence.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of soft engineering?
A) Sea wall
B) Rock armour
C) Beach nourishment
D) Groyne
practice_questions.marks: C) Beach nourishment [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of a managed retreat scheme.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for a developed description, e.g.:
• A sea wall is deliberately breached so the sea floods low-lying land behind it (1), creating a salt marsh that absorbs wave energy before it reaches a new defence built further inland (1).
• Low-value farmland is allowed to flood (1) so that the wider area, including more valuable settlements, is protected at lower long-term cost (1).
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why some coastlines are protected with hard engineering while others are not.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks for a developed cause-effect explanation:
• Cost-benefit analysis (1) compares the cost of building defences with the value of the property and infrastructure being protected (1).
• Coastlines with high-value land uses such as town centres, ports or tourist resorts (e.g. Cromer) are defended because the benefit outweighs the cost (1).
• Lower-value, sparsely populated stretches (e.g. parts of Happisburgh) receive no active intervention because defending them is not economically justified (1).
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Compare hard engineering and soft engineering as ways of protecting UK coastlines.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Credit explicit comparison words (whereas, in contrast, similarly):
• Hard engineering uses large built structures such as sea walls and groynes, whereas soft engineering uses natural processes such as beach nourishment and dune regeneration (1).
• Hard engineering has a high upfront cost (sea wall around £5,000/m), in contrast soft engineering is usually cheaper but needs regular topping up (1).
• Hard engineering protects high-value areas quickly; in contrast soft engineering is more sustainable and protects ecosystems (1).
• Both approaches can be used together within an ICZM plan to balance protection and sustainability (1).
[4 marks — must include explicit comparison links to gain full marks]

practice_questions.text: Using a named example, explain how managed retreat can reduce coastal flood risk.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks for a fully developed explanation with locational detail:
• Identifies a named scheme such as Medmerry (West Sussex, 2013) or the Essex coast (1).
• Describes the action: an existing sea wall was breached and 183 hectares of farmland flooded (1).
• A new flood defence was built up to 2 km inland to protect properties further back from the coast (1).
• Explains how the new salt marsh absorbs wave energy and storm surges before they reach the new defence, reducing flood risk (1).
• Notes the protected outcome: 348 properties in the village of Selsey area are now safer (1).
• Adds long-term benefit: marsh creates habitat, lowers maintenance cost compared with constantly repairing the original sea wall (1).
[6 marks — locational detail and named example are essential for top marks]

practice_questions.text:
'The most sustainable way to manage UK coastlines is managed retreat.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation weighing managed retreat against hard engineering. Uses named examples (e.g. Medmerry success, Happisburgh, Mappleton's downstream impact) and explicit linking words. Reaches a justified conclusion (e.g. managed retreat is most sustainable on low-value coasts but inappropriate for high-value urban shorelines).

Secure: Clear arguments for and against, supported by at least one UK example. Conclusion is reached but may be partly asserted rather than fully justified.

Developing: Some arguments on each side but examples are generic ('a UK coastline'). Limited weighing — points are listed rather than judged.

Emerging: Simple comments on managed retreat with little evaluation; examples missing or inaccurate.

Arguments in support: lower long-term cost; works with natural processes; creates salt-marsh habitat; reduces wave energy reaching settlements; copes better with sea level rise.
Arguments against: loses farmland and homes; emotional/political opposition; not viable for high-value land (Cromer, Blackpool); compensation costs; risks if storm surge exceeds new defence.
[8 marks + 4 SPaG]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes a discordant coastline?
A) Rock bands run parallel to the sea
B) Rock bands run at right angles to the sea
C) Rocks are entirely made of chalk
D) Rocks are entirely made of clay
practice_questions.marks: B) Rock bands run at right angles to the sea [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two characteristics of a concordant coast.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Rock bands lie parallel to the line of the coast.
• Cliffs tend to be straight and continuous over long distances.
• A single rock type often forms most of the cliff face.
• Bays form only after a hard outer band is breached, exposing softer rocks behind (e.g. Lulworth Cove).
[2 marks — 1 per characteristic]

practice_questions.text: Explain how fetch affects coastal erosion.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Fetch is the distance the wind blows over open sea before reaching the coast.
• A longer fetch lets waves grow taller and carry more energy by the time they break on the cliff.
• Coasts facing the Atlantic — like Cornwall — receive much higher-energy waves than those facing the short fetch of the Irish Sea, so erosion is faster.
[3 marks. Mastering: full chain of reasoning. Secure: defines fetch and links to wave energy. Developing: defines fetch only. Emerging: confuses with frequency or wind direction.]

practice_questions.text: Compare how geology and human activity affect rates of coastal erosion.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Geology fixes the long-term rate (hard rocks erode slowly, soft rocks fast), whereas human activity changes the rate over decades by adding or removing defences.
• Geology is uncontrollable, in contrast to human activity which can be planned and reversed.
• Both can produce the same outcome — accelerated erosion — but for different reasons (weak rock vs starved sediment supply).
• Human defences sometimes interact with geology, e.g. groynes only work where there is mobile sediment to trap.
[4 marks — credit explicit comparison.]

practice_questions.text: Using a named UK example, explain how human activity has changed rates of erosion along a coast.
practice_questions.marks:
Mappleton (Holderness coast) is suitable. Students may include:
• Mappleton is a small village on the East Yorkshire coast where soft boulder clay cliffs were retreating at around 2 metres per year.
• In 1991, two large rock groynes were built to trap sand and protect the village.
• The groynes succeeded locally — Mappleton’s cliff stabilised and the road and houses were saved.
• However, the groynes blocked southward longshore drift, starving cliffs at Cowden and Aldbrough of sand.
• Erosion at those villages then accelerated, with farmland and roads lost; this is sometimes called terminal groyne syndrome.
• The example shows that human action transferred erosion rather than removing it.

Mastering: developed explanation, named place, multiple linked impacts.
Secure: clear sequence with example.
Developing: outcome described but cause-effect unclear.
Emerging: generic ‘defences cause problems’ with no place.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
‘Geology is the most important factor controlling rates of landform change in the UK.’
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Geology fixes long-term resistance — hard chalk at Seven Sisters loses centimetres a year, soft Holderness clay loses metres.
• Concordant and discordant arrangements decide where headlands, bays and coves form.
• Without geological contrast, the variety of UK landforms would not exist.

Arguments against:
• Climate determines the energy attacking the rock; the same rock erodes faster on a stormy west coast than a sheltered east coast.
• Human activity can transform a coast in years rather than millennia, e.g. Mappleton groynes.
• Climate change is currently increasing storm frequency and sea level — both will speed up erosion regardless of rock type.

Judgement: a strong answer argues that geology sets the long-term rate, but climate triggers most of the actual change, and human activity can override both for short stretches.

Mastering: sustained evaluation, examples, clear conclusion.
Secure: balanced arguments with examples.
Developing: imbalanced or weak conclusion.
Emerging: list with no judgement.
[8 marks + 4 SPaG]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the largest single driver of Amazon deforestation?
A) Mining
B) Cattle ranching and soya
C) Tourism
D) Forest fires from natural causes
practice_questions.marks: B) Cattle ranching and soya [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways monoculture farming damages tropical soils.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark for each developed point, up to 2:
• Bare soil between rows is exposed to heavy tropical rainfall, leading to high rates of soil erosion (1).
• A single crop draws the same nutrients each year, gradually exhausting the soil and increasing the need for fertiliser (1).
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why deforestation in the Amazon reduces regional rainfall.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks for a clear cause-effect chain:
• Rainforest trees release huge volumes of water vapour through evapotranspiration (1).
• This water vapour rises, condenses and produces convective rainfall over the rainforest itself (1).
• When trees are removed, evapotranspiration falls — local atmospheric moisture drops and regional rainfall declines (around 25% in parts of the southern Amazon) (1).
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Compare the impacts of human activity on the Amazon rainforest with those on the African savanna.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Credit explicit comparison words:
• In the Amazon, the dominant impact is deforestation for cattle and soya, whereas on the savanna it is overgrazing by domestic cattle and expansion of crop fields (1).
• Both biomes lose biodiversity, in contrast the Amazon's losses are dominated by tree-dwelling species while the savanna's are dominated by large mammals such as elephants (1).
• Soil erosion accelerates in both, similarly because vegetation cover is reduced — but rainforest soils thin to nutrient-poor laterite, whereas savanna soils form dust that blows away in the dry season (1).
• Climate change is amplifying impacts in both — drier dry seasons in the Amazon and longer droughts on the savanna (1).
[4 marks — must include explicit comparison links]

practice_questions.text: Using a named example, explain how energy production can damage an ecosystem.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks for a developed answer with locational detail:
• Names a specific scheme such as the Belo Monte HEP dam in Brazil, the London Array offshore wind farm or the proposed Swansea Bay tidal lagoon (1).
• Gives a key statistic: Belo Monte drowned 668 km² of forest / Swansea Bay would have built a 9.5 km sea wall (1).
• Identifies a habitat or species impact: loss of indigenous land and submerged forest at Belo Monte / disrupted salmon and sea-trout migration at Swansea Bay (1).
• Explains a process: rotting submerged biomass at Belo Monte emits methane / construction noise from offshore wind farms disturbs harbour porpoises (1).
• Notes a wider environmental consequence: reduced river flow downstream / changed sediment movement in the bay (1).
• Acknowledges the trade-off: clean energy benefits weighed against ecosystem cost — a balance the exam explicitly tests (1).
[6 marks — locational detail and named example are essential]

practice_questions.text:
'It is impossible to meet the world's energy needs without damaging ecosystems.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Use the StudyVault rubric.

Mastering: Sustained evaluation comparing fossil fuels (climate change), HEP (Belo Monte forest loss), wind (London Array marine impacts), tidal (Swansea Bay rejected) and solar (land use trade-offs). Reaches a justified conclusion that all energy systems impose some ecosystem cost, but renewables impose far less than fossil fuels.

Secure: Clear arguments for and against. Some named examples. Conclusion partly asserted.

Developing: Some arguments on each side; examples generic. Limited weighing.

Emerging: Simple comments on energy with no comparison and no examples.

In favour: every form of energy production reshapes habitats; renewables still need land and materials; HEP drowns forests; offshore wind disturbs marine life; mining for solar panels causes pollution.
Against: well-sited renewables (rooftop solar, repowered turbines) impose minimal damage; energy efficiency reduces total demand; comparing per-kWh ecosystem cost shows renewables are far less harmful than coal.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes an out-of-town retail park?
A) A traditional shopping street in the centre of a town
B) A large retail centre on the edge of a town with extensive free parking
C) A small parade of shops next to a housing estate
D) A weekly outdoor market in a market square
practice_questions.marks: B) A large retail centre on the edge of a town with extensive free parking [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two reasons why UK internet shopping has grown rapidly since 2010.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for each reason described, up to two:
• Faster broadband and smartphone use let customers research, compare and buy from anywhere.
• Same-day and next-day delivery networks remove the need to visit shops.
• Covid-19 lockdowns from March 2020 forced non-essential shops to close, accelerating online use.
• Price-comparison sites push prices down and make online cheaper than high-street equivalents.
• Younger shoppers expect a digital-first experience.
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why some UK high streets have lost shoppers in the last twenty years.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Three reasons explained with cause-effect chains and named context (e.g. out-of-town parks like the Metro Centre offer free parking, internet shopping at 26% of sales pulls trade online, department-store collapses such as Debenhams leave gaps).
Secure: Two clear reasons explained.
Developing: Two reasons stated with limited explanation.
Emerging: One reason with little explanation.
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Compare shopping at an out-of-town retail park with shopping on a traditional UK high street.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained comparison using linking words (whereas, in contrast, similarly). Both settings covered with specific detail — out-of-town free parking and longer hours, contrasted with high-street pedestrian access, mix of independents and lower car emissions.
Secure: Clear comparison with relevant detail for both.
Developing: Some comparison; describes each setting separately.
Emerging: One setting described; little or no comparison.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Using a UK case study, explain how a town or city has tried to revive its high street.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A named UK case study (e.g. Stockton-on-Tees) with specific evidence — 19% vacancy rate, Globe theatre reopened 2021 (3,000 capacity), Castlegate centre demolished 2023, Shambles for independents — linked to at least two reasons the actions help (footfall, mixed use, reduced reliance on chain retail).
Secure: Named place with detail and at least two explained changes.
Developing: Some place-specific detail; one change explained.
Emerging: General reference to high-street change with no named place.
[6 marks — locational detail is essential]

practice_questions.text: 'The growth of internet shopping has done more harm than good to UK towns and cities.' Evaluate this statement. Reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support (more harm):
• Online sales reaching 26% of UK retail in 2024 has cut high-street footfall, contributing to chain failures (Debenhams, BHS, Wilko).
• Empty units lower the appeal and tax base of towns; vacancy rates around 14% nationally.
• Delivery vans add traffic and emissions in residential streets.

Arguments against (more good):
• Customers in rural areas with poor transport now have access to the same range as cities.
• Lower prices benefit lower-income households.
• High streets are reinventing themselves as leisure and mixed-use spaces (Stockton's Globe theatre, Castlegate park) — a positive shift, not a death.
• Online retailers create jobs (Amazon UK over 75,000) and new fulfilment centres support post-industrial regions.

Mastering: Sophisticated argument with both sides developed using named places, weighted judgement and a justified conclusion.
Secure: Both sides argued with relevant evidence and a clear conclusion.
Developing: One side stronger; conclusion stated but limited justification.
Emerging: Simple points; little judgement.
[8 marks + 4 SPaG]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the informal economy?
A) Trade carried out only between large multinational companies
B) Small-scale, unregistered businesses that are not regulated or taxed
C) Government-run shops and services in a city centre
D) Online shopping completed through registered platforms
practice_questions.marks: B) Small-scale, unregistered businesses that are not regulated or taxed [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways in which Mumbai is connected to the rest of the world.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for each connection described, up to two:
• Bollywood is the world's largest film industry by volume, exporting Indian culture worldwide.
• Jawaharlal Nehru Port, in the Mumbai region, is one of India's biggest container ports.
• Chhatrapati Shivaji International Airport handled over 50 million passengers in 2019.
• Mumbai is the headquarters of the Reserve Bank of India and a major financial centre for South Asia.
• Migration from across South Asia and the Indian diaspora connects the city worldwide.
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why London continues to grow in population.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Three reasons explained with cause-effect chains and named detail (e.g. international migration drawn by financial-sector jobs in the City; world-leading universities pulling students; English-language advantage; over 40% of Londoners born outside the UK).
Secure: Two reasons clearly explained.
Developing: Two reasons stated with limited explanation.
Emerging: One reason with little explanation.
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Compare the way of life in London with the way of life in Mumbai.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained comparison using linking words. Both cities covered with named detail (Kensington vs Tower Hamlets, Antilia vs Dharavi; average house prices £530,000 vs Dharavi 700,000 residents in 2 sq km).
Secure: Both cities named with relevant detail; clear comparison.
Developing: Two places mentioned but described separately.
Emerging: One city described; little or no comparison.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Using a named LIC or NIC city, explain how rural-to-urban migration has shaped its growth.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A named LIC/NIC city (e.g. Mumbai) with specific evidence — population growth from 12m in 1990 to 21m today, around 1,000 arrivals daily, push factors (drought, small landholdings) and pull factors (docks, Bollywood, IT) — linked to at least two consequences (Dharavi housing pressure, informal economy, Bandra-Kurla Complex jobs).
Secure: Named city with detail and at least two explained consequences.
Developing: Some place-specific detail; one consequence explained.
Emerging: General reference to migration with no place-specific detail.
[6 marks — locational detail is essential]

practice_questions.text: 'The challenges faced by global cities in HICs and LICs/NICs are essentially the same.' Evaluate this statement using London and Mumbai. Reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support (similar challenges):
• Both cities face extreme inequality between richest and poorest neighbourhoods (Kensington vs Tower Hamlets in London; Antilia vs Dharavi in Mumbai).
• Both must provide affordable housing under heavy population pressure.
• Both face air pollution and traffic congestion.

Arguments against (different challenges):
• Mumbai's main housing problem is informal settlement (700,000 in Dharavi alone) — London's is unaffordable formal housing (165,000 in temporary accommodation).
• Around 60% of Mumbai's workers are in the informal economy with no protection; London's labour market is overwhelmingly formal.
• Mumbai's population growth is driven by internal rural-to-urban migration; London's by international migration.
• Climate vulnerability differs — Mumbai faces monsoon flooding on a scale London does not.

Mastering: Sophisticated argument with both sides developed using named places and figures, weighted judgement and a justified conclusion.
Secure: Both sides argued with relevant evidence and a clear conclusion.
Developing: One side stronger; conclusion stated but limited justification.
Emerging: Simple points; little judgement.
[8 marks + 4 SPaG]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a flow within a drainage basin?
A) Vegetation store
B) Interception
C) Lake store
D) Groundwater store
practice_questions.marks: B) Interception [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of a flashy hydrograph.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• A short lag time between peak rainfall and peak discharge.
• A steep rising limb showing rapid arrival of water in the channel.
• A high peak discharge relative to the channel’s usual flow.
• A steep falling limb as the storm runoff passes quickly through the basin.
[2 marks — 1 per feature]

practice_questions.text: Explain how urbanisation increases the risk of river flooding.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Buildings, roads and car parks replace grass and soil with impermeable surfaces, so rain cannot infiltrate.
• Drains and gutters move water quickly into rivers, shortening lag time.
• Higher peak discharge means rivers more easily exceed channel capacity and spill onto floodplains.
[3 marks. Mastering: full causal chain. Secure: identifies impermeable surfaces and faster runoff. Developing: one mechanism. Emerging: vague ‘more buildings means more flooding’.]

practice_questions.text: Compare the responses of a forested rural basin and an urban basin to the same heavy rainstorm.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• In the forested basin, interception slows rainfall reaching the ground; in the urban basin, almost no interception occurs.
• Infiltration is high in rural soils, whereas urban surfaces force most water to run off as overland flow.
• Lag time is long in the rural basin, in contrast to the short lag in the urban basin.
• Peak discharge is moderate in the rural basin but sharp and high in the urban basin.
[4 marks — credit explicit comparison.]

practice_questions.text: Using a named UK example, explain the physical and human causes of a flood event.
practice_questions.marks:
Calder Valley 2015 is suitable. Students may include:
• Storm Eva delivered over 100 mm of rain to the upper Calder catchment in 24 hours.
• Soils were already saturated from heavy rain earlier in December, so almost all the new rain became runoff.
• Steep narrow valleys funnelled water rapidly into the River Calder.
• Drainage of upland moor for grouse shooting had reduced peat’s ability to hold water.
• Hebden Bridge and Mytholmroyd lie directly on the floodplain, so when defences were overtopped about 2,000 homes flooded and damage exceeded £100 million.

Mastering: developed explanation, named place, multiple linked causes.
Secure: clear sequence with example.
Developing: cause described but located detail thin.
Emerging: generic answer with no UK example.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
‘Human activity is more important than physical conditions in causing UK river flooding.’
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Building on floodplains in cities like Carlisle and York places people directly in the flood path.
• Urbanisation creates impermeable surfaces, sharpening flood peaks.
• Drainage of upland peat (e.g. Calderdale) removes natural water storage.
• Channelisation and removal of meanders speed water downstream into towns.

Arguments against:
• Even fully natural basins flood when heavy rain falls on saturated soil.
• Climate change is increasing rainfall intensity beyond what land use alone can explain.
• Geology (impermeable rock) and topography (steep slopes) determine flood-proneness.
• The 2015 floods affected forested upland valleys as well as urban centres.

Judgement: a strong response argues that physical conditions create the flood potential while human activity decides how much harm it does — both are needed.

Mastering: sustained evaluation, named places, clear conclusion.
Secure: arguments on both sides with examples.
Developing: one-sided.
Emerging: list with no judgement.
[8 marks + 4 SPaG]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes a positive multiplier effect?
A) The negative impact of factory closures on a town
B) A chain reaction in which one positive change generates further growth in jobs and services
C) A government policy of charging higher taxes in richer regions
D) The geographical distance between London and the north of England
practice_questions.marks: B) A chain reaction in which one positive change generates further growth in jobs and services [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the UK north-south divide.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: a clear feature with brief development, e.g. average incomes and life expectancy are higher in London and the south-east than in parts of the north, illustrated by the Blackpool-Hart male life expectancy gap of over ten years. Secure: feature identified with limited development. Developing: vague reference to inequality. Emerging: no specific feature.

practice_questions.text: Explain how negative multipliers can affect a UK region.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: a clear chain — major employer closes, workers lose jobs, less spending in local shops and services, those businesses close too, tax revenue falls, schools and services are cut, young people move away. Secure: one mechanism with effect. Developing: states the area gets worse without explanation. Emerging: no causal link.

practice_questions.text: Compare infrastructure investment and urban regeneration as ways to reduce UK regional inequality.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: explicit comparison using linking words on at least two points — both create jobs and aim to rebalance the country, however infrastructure works at national scale (HS2 connecting cities) whereas regeneration works on a single site (Salford Quays brownfield site); infrastructure is delivered over decades whereas regeneration delivers visible change within a few years. Secure: one explicit comparison. Developing: lists features separately. Emerging: only one feature named.

practice_questions.text: Explain how investment can help reduce regional inequality in the UK. Use named examples.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: developed account with named projects (HS2, Salford Quays MediaCityUK, Cardiff Bay, Northern Powerhouse Rail) covering at least two strategies and how positive multipliers work — new jobs, supplier firms, tax revenue, knock-on services, regenerated brownfield sites. Secure: named example with two strategies but limited detail. Developing: generic with one strategy. Emerging: vague reference without named place.

practice_questions.text:
“Investment in transport infrastructure is the best way to rebalance the UK.”
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument with named examples weighing benefits of transport investment (HS2 cutting journey times, Northern Powerhouse Rail linking cities, multipliers from new jobs) against limits (cost, possible pull of jobs back to London, slow delivery) and against alternatives (urban regeneration like Salford Quays/Cardiff Bay, devolution to mayors, levelling-up grants, skills funding) reaching a justified judgement (e.g. transport works only when combined with skills and local powers). Secure: balanced argument with one named example. Developing: one-sided or generic. Emerging: simple agreement or disagreement without evidence.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of sustainable management of a tropical rainforest?
A) Clearing forest for cattle ranches
B) Selective logging certified by the FSC
C) Building a hydroelectric dam reservoir
D) Burning forest to plant soya
practice_questions.marks: B) Selective logging certified by the FSC [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by ecotourism.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks for a developed description:
• Travel that focuses on natural environments and tries to fund conservation rather than cause damage (1).
• Often supports local people through jobs as guides, rangers or hospitality staff so that protecting the ecosystem is more profitable than destroying it (1).
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how zoning within a National Park supports sustainable management.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks for a clear cause-effect chain:
• Zoning divides the park into areas with different levels of protection (1).
• The strictest zones (e.g. nesting beaches in Tortuguero) prevent disturbance of vulnerable species (1).
• Buffer or use zones allow controlled tourism or low-impact farming, raising income that funds conservation in the strict zones (1).
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Compare ecotourism and selective logging as strategies to manage tropical rainforests.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Credit explicit comparison words:
• Ecotourism earns income from visitors enjoying intact forest, whereas selective logging earns income from removing high-value trees (1).
• Ecotourism leaves the canopy completely undisturbed, in contrast selective logging takes some mature trees but leaves the canopy mostly intact (1).
• Both can support local jobs, similarly providing alternatives to clearing forest for agriculture (1).
• Both depend on enforcement — ecotourism on managing visitor numbers, in contrast selective logging on FSC certification preventing over-cutting (1).
[4 marks — must include explicit comparison links]

practice_questions.text: Using a named example, explain how a country has used sustainable strategies to protect its rainforest.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks for a developed answer with locational detail:
• Names a country, e.g. Costa Rica (1).
• Identifies a strategy: National Park network protecting around 25% of national territory (1).
• Identifies a second strategy: Payments for Ecosystem Services rewarding landowners to keep forest standing (1).
• Adds an ecotourism dimension: about 60% of tourists visit for nature-based holidays (1).
• Provides outcome data: forest cover rose from 25% in 1985 to about 60% today (1).
• Notes a wider economic benefit: tourism revenue exceeded US$4 billion in 2019, making forest protection profitable (1).
[6 marks — locational detail and named example are essential]

practice_questions.text:
'Sustainable management of tropical rainforests is impossible without rich countries paying for it.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Use the StudyVault rubric.

Mastering: Sustained evaluation weighing international funding (REDD+, Norway's payments to Brazil) against domestic strategies (Costa Rica's PES, Brazilian indigenous reserves, agro-forestry). Uses named numbers and reaches a justified conclusion (e.g. external funding can accelerate change but lasting success depends on domestic enforcement and incentives).

Secure: Clear arguments for and against. Some named examples and figures. Conclusion partly asserted.

Developing: Some arguments on each side; examples generic. Limited weighing.

Emerging: Simple comments on funding with no comparison and no examples.

In favour: REDD+ paid Brazil over US$1.2 billion since 2008; Costa Rica's PES initially funded by World Bank loans; LICs lack tax revenue to protect forests alone; carbon markets shift cost to high-emitters.
Against: Costa Rica largely self-funds its scheme; community conservancies in Kenya generate their own income; over-reliance on aid creates dependency; payments are hard to verify; some success comes from indigenous land rights, not money.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of soft engineering?
A) A concrete flood wall through a city centre
B) A demountable barrier slotted into permanent foundations
C) Planting trees in an upland catchment to slow runoff
D) Straightening a meandering channel
practice_questions.marks: C) Planting trees in an upland catchment to slow runoff [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of land-use zoning on a UK floodplain.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The Environment Agency divides floodplains into zones from 1 (lowest risk) to 3b (highest risk).
• New homes are normally restricted to Zone 1 or 2.
• Lower-value uses such as parks, playing fields and car parks are placed in higher-risk zones.
• Planning policy aims that when the river floods, it floods green space rather than housing.
[2 marks — 1 per feature]

practice_questions.text: Explain how soft engineering reduces flood risk.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Trees intercept rainfall and let it evaporate or drip slowly to the soil.
• Soils with strong root structure infiltrate water rather than letting it run off.
• Leaky dams and ponds in upland streams hold floodwater back, reducing peak discharge in towns downstream.
[3 marks. Mastering: full causal chain. Secure: clear mechanism. Developing: identifies a method. Emerging: vague.]

practice_questions.text: Compare the costs and benefits of hard and soft engineering.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Hard engineering provides immediate, high-level protection in dense urban areas; soft engineering offers gradual, distributed protection across catchments.
• Hard engineering is generally far more expensive (£millions per scheme) than soft engineering, which can be tens of thousands.
• Soft engineering creates wildlife habitat, whereas hard engineering can damage river ecology.
• Hard engineering can fail catastrophically when overtopped; soft engineering rarely fails dramatically but cannot stop the largest floods alone.
[4 marks — credit explicit comparison.]

practice_questions.text: Using a named UK example, explain how a flood management scheme has reduced flood risk.
practice_questions.marks:
Belford Burn (Northumberland) is suitable. Students may include:
• The scheme installed around 35 small woody dams in upland tributaries, plus ponds and wetlands, to hold around 6,000 m³ of floodwater.
• Each leaky dam slows runoff so peak discharge in Belford village is reduced by about 30 %.
• The scheme cost less than £350,000, a fraction of typical hard engineering schemes.
• It also restored habitat for fish, insects and water voles, providing wider ecological benefits.
• Combined with limited hard defences in the village itself, the scheme protects homes that previously flooded repeatedly.

Mastering: developed explanation, named scheme, multiple linked impacts.
Secure: clear sequence with example.
Developing: outcome described but located detail thin.
Emerging: generic ‘soft engineering works’ with no place.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
‘Hard engineering is the only effective way to manage flood risk in UK cities.’
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Dense city centres like Carlisle have nowhere for floodwater to go safely; only walls and barriers can hold it back.
• Protecting historic infrastructure (rail, power, hospitals) requires immediate, large-scale defences.
• Hard engineering produces measurable protection — Carlisle’s £38 million scheme prevents floods in design-level events.
• Demountable barriers offer reliable urban protection without permanent visual impact.

Arguments against:
• Hard engineering is expensive and shifts flooding downstream when overtopped.
• Soft engineering and natural flood management (Belford, Calderdale) reduce peak flows for a fraction of the cost.
• Land-use zoning prevents new urban damage at almost no cost.
• Climate change makes design-level walls obsolete faster, so hybrid solutions are essential.

Judgement: a strong response argues that hard engineering is necessary for the most valuable areas but should be combined with upstream soft measures and zoning to be sustainable in the long run.

Mastering: sustained evaluation, named places, clear conclusion.
Secure: arguments on both sides with examples.
Developing: imbalanced or weak conclusion.
Emerging: list with no judgement.
[8 marks + 4 SPaG]
